title: http: enforce the JVM attempt timeout through response-body consumption
description:
Enforce the JVM managed HTTP attempt deadline through response-body consumption, cancelling the underlying exchange when the deadline expires. HttpRequest.timeout currently stops protecting the attempt after response headers, so a stalled body defeats the advertised finite deadline and can later return success.

Surface: impl_http. Parent: rf2-gwye. SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2. WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review). Revalidated against baseline 9e8ca973767f4ecff455421e48e1765d59783261 on 2026-09-13. This is the independent timeout finding split from aggregate rf2-fzbj.11; it is independent of anonymous frame ownership and affects identified requests too.

## Evidence and contract

- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport_jvm.cljc:167-168 stamps only HttpRequest.Builder.timeout.
- transport_jvm.cljc:283-310 calls sendAsync with BodyHandlers.ofByteArray and transforms its full-body future with thenApply. There is no independent timer covering completion of that future.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc:2032-2101 measures elapsed time and classifies exceptional completion, but does not enforce a deadline around the body future.
- In contrast, implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport_cljs.cljc:226-283 races fetch plus read-body against a timer and cleans that timer on settlement.
- spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:146 calls timeout-ms a per-attempt wall-clock timeout; 305-316 supplies a 30000 ms default with explicit nil/0 opt-outs. Line 307 specifically promises protection from upstreams that never complete a response body. This finding concerns a single network attempt, not an overall retry budget or timing arbitrary user body-preparation code.

## Real transport reproducer and fresh result

On installed JDK 21.0.10, start a loopback com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer on an ephemeral port. The handler sends 200 with Content-Length: 2, writes and flushes byte A, signals a started latch, then holds byte B behind a release latch with a finite backstop. Call production jvm-fetch with {:method :get :url <loopback-url> :decode :text :timeout-ms 500}.

After server entry, get the returned future with an independent 1500 ms observation limit. Fresh result: still-pending-after-ms=1508. No framework timeout occurred although the configured budget elapsed three times. Release B: the SAME future succeeds with {:ok? true :status 200 :body-text "AB"}, plus normal metadata.

Control: the same loopback server stalls BEFORE headers with the same 500 ms request timeout. The real production future completes exceptionally with java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException; measured elapsed 881 ms including setup/scheduling. Thus the configured timer and failure classifier are live, while the body phase escapes them. The 1500 ms limit in the failing case is the probe's future.get observation timeout, not a framework timeout.

Expected: if the positive per-attempt budget expires before body consumption completes, cancel the underlying request and settle once through the existing :rf.http/timeout category, including elapsed-ms/limit-ms and configured timeout retries. Actual: a promptly headed stalled/trickling body can hold futures, buffers, handles and request concurrency without triggering timeout-based retry, or deliver success after the declared deadline.

## Suggested repair and acceptance

Use an attempt-local deadline covering the actual sendAsync/body-consumption future; on expiry cancel its underlying JDK exchange and classify through the existing canonical timeout path. Cancel/detach the timer on normal success, failure and manual/lifecycle abort. Preserve nil/0 opt-out, per-retry rearming, abort precedence and exactly-one-terminal-reply behavior. A result-only future timeout that leaves host work running is insufficient. Keep this change within the existing API; do not add an overall retry-sequence timeout or body-thunk interruption.

- Add a real JVM adapter regression sending headers and the first body byte promptly, then stalling beyond a small positive timeout. It must time out while the body is still held and cancel host work; the current baseline must fail.
- Delayed-before-headers still times out, a complete response inside the budget succeeds, and nil/0 retain the documented opt-out.
- Late body completion after timeout cannot emit success or a duplicate reply. Configured timeout retries are rearmed once per attempt.
- Manual/frame/actor abort racing the timer preserves the existing classification and suppression semantics; every terminal path releases timer resources.
- Both text and binary decode use the whole-body deadline. No browser behavior change is required; preserve CLJS parity.

## Validation and deduplication

Executed fresh actual-adapter loopback witness in ai/surface-review-20260913/impl_http/probe-impl_http-1.clj/.log/.exit, exit 0, using only cached dependencies (Clojure 1.12.4, JDK 21.0.10). It printed the production transport_jvm.cljc resource URL under SOURCE_ROOT. The server had an ephemeral port and finite waits; exchange close, latch release, future cancellation and server stop ran through finally, and the disposable JVM exited. The decisive outcomes and a complete recipe are above; ignored scratch is supplemental only.

Inspected current adapter/error classifier, shared attempt callback, retry handoffs, terminal-once logic and CLJS whole-body race. Existing http_transport_security_test.clj:94-192 checks the HttpRequest timeout attribute. The timeout witness in http_jvm_binary_decode_test.clj:184 onward delays before headers. Neither demonstrates bounded body consumption. No production edits, dependency install, shared build, broad gate, browser execution or exhaustive JDK-version matrix was performed. The real delayed-body witness used text; byte-array collection is shared with binary, but binary timeout behavior was not separately executed.

Read current aggregate rf2-fzbj.11 and three newest history records; no correction supersedes F2. Current all-status HTTP/anonymous/timeout title search plus checkpoint-body search found no identical dedicated open owner. rf2-fzbj.24's body-read finding concerns the separate ssr-ring Node crossing, not this managed HTTP adapter. Closed rf2-rsv2n repairs abort during preparation/issuance and remains closed; a stalled response after issuance is a distinct phase. Keep the original aggregate unchanged.
notes:
=== VERDICT (worker http-a, 2026-09-13): FIXED in PR #9745 (commit c0e893b339 on worker/http-a, branched at 031ff49a38). This is finding F2 of rf2-fzbj.11, fixed once for both beads. ===
Re-verified at that base before fixing: it reproduced as described.

The fix: jvm-fetch arms CompletableFuture.orTimeout(:timeout-ms) on the future it returns. When the deadline fires (TimeoutException), it also cancels the upstream sendAsync future, and that cancellation is what closes the JDK exchange. classify-jvm-error maps java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException to :rf.http/timeout, carrying :elapsed-ms and :limit-ms.
- nil and 0 still arm nothing.
- Each retry calls jvm-fetch afresh, so it re-arms its own budget.
- The JDK withdraws the deadline on any other completion, including a lifecycle abort's cancel.
Measured before choosing this shape: an orTimeout on the result alone completed at the deadline, but the loopback server still streamed the whole 8 MB body. Adding the upstream cancel made the server's next write fail at once.

Regression test: implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_jvm_body_timeout_test.clj. A loopback HttpServer sends headers and one byte, then withholds an 8 MB body behind a latch. A managed request with :timeout-ms 200 and one timeout retry must:
- reply :rf.http/timeout at attempt 2, with :limit-ms 200 and elapsed >= 200, while the body is still withheld;
- have both exchanges cancelled server-side (the write fails after release);
- produce no late or duplicate reply.
Pre-fix: no reply within 5 s, so the test was red. There is also an opt-out guard: :timeout-ms 0 and nil stay pending, then succeed on release.

Gates: jvm-http exit 0 (505 tests / 4015 assertions); the existing delayed-before-headers test is in that run.

Skipped suggestions, one sentence each:
- Abort racing the timer: precedence lives in the unchanged :aborted?/:finalised? cells, and the deadline completes through the same whenComplete -> maybe-retry! route the JDK's HttpTimeoutException already used.
- Binary-reader timeout executed separately: binary reads the same ofByteArray future the deadline wraps.
- A new delayed-before-headers control: the existing jvm-real-timeout-populates-elapsed-ms already covers it.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #9745 (commit c0e893b339), together with its aggregate rf2-fzbj.11. F1, anonymous frame ownership: the registry indexes requests with neither id under their issuing frame (anonymous-in-flight); they are removed by identity and read-and-cleared by the frame-destroy / epoch-restore sweep. F2, the JVM timeout: jvm-fetch arms orTimeout over the whole attempt, cancels the upstream sendAsync on expiry, and TimeoutException classifies as :rf.http/timeout. Both have regression tests shown red on pre-fix code; the jvm-http and CLJS node-test gates exit 0. The skipped suggestions and their one-sentence reasons are in the notes.

title: fresco: release React root when initial Hiccup lowering throws
description:
Release the newly allocated React root if first-render Hiccup lowering throws. This is a bounded failed-construction repair: preserve the caller's exception, leave the container available for an ordinary retry, and keep the successful public client-root lifecycle unchanged.

Surface: impl_fresco; implementation/fresco/**. Revalidated at 9e8ca973767f4ecff455421e48e1765d59783261 on 2026-09-13. SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2. WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review).

Confirmed path

- implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/mount.cljs:248-257: root! calls createRoot before render! and has no failed-construction cleanup.
- The same file:107: render! evaluates (tree handle hiccup) before invoking the raw Root's .render.
- implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/codec.cljs:1278-1295 and :1821-1866: root-element/as-element synchronously realize supported lazy child sequences.
- mount.cljs:527-533 and :553-558: active-root tracking and publication into the opaque public handle occur only after root! returns. :561-569 makes public unmount! a no-op when that publication never happened.

Concrete trigger

With the usual adapter initialized and a DOM container attached, using [re-frame.fresco :as h]:

(def root (h/client-root))
(def boom (js/Error. "row formatting failed"))
(def rows (map (fn [_] (throw boom)) [1]))
(try (h/render! root [:ul rows] container)
     (catch :default e (assert (identical? boom e))))
(h/unmount! root)
(h/render! root [:div "recovered"] container)

The Hiccup vector and lazy child sequence are valid. A normal user computation fails while formatting a row. This is not malformed input or a throwing component body reported later by React. React already owns the container, but Fresco loses the newly returned Root handle before publishing it. Public unmount! and the active-root drain cannot reach it. A retry calls createRoot again against an already-rooted container and produces React's duplicate-root warning in development; abandoning the mount leaves an untracked root on that container. No claim is made that this pre-render failure commits child effects or subscriptions.

Expected versus actual

Expected: propagate the original first-render exception and release any ownership acquired by the failed construction. A corrected render through the same public handle mounts normally and unmounts once.
Actual: root ownership begins before lowering, while the only public cleanup ownership begins after lowering. The exception escapes through the gap.

Suggested repair

Prefer lowering the initial element before createRoot takes ownership if that keeps the code simple; alternatively catch a synchronous first-render failure after allocation, unmount that exact new Root, and rethrow the original exception. Preserve root options, update behavior, opaque handles and active-set liveness. Hydrate-root! already builds its element before hydrateRoot, so this finding does not call for rewriting hydration or changing React's component-error policy.

Acceptance criteria

1. Add a red public h/client-root/h/render! regression with a valid lazy child computation throwing during first lowering; observe the exact thrown object and prove no allocated root remains unowned. Constructor/unmount spies can establish exact ownership.
2. Include a DOM retry through the same handle that succeeds with no duplicate-createRoot warning; final unmount releases that root once, and an intervening unmount after the failure is safe.
3. Retain existing create-once/update-later, post-disposal remount and adapter-disposal lifecycle witnesses.

Validation and limits

Fresh source-path trace against the stated revision; client_root_lifecycle_dom_cljs_test.cljs and public_root_lifecycle_dom_cljs_test.cljs inspected, not executed. A process-local Node witness exercised installed React 19.3.0 directly with an in-memory DOM-shaped container: a createRoot with no render already marks the container; a second createRoot produces the real duplicate-root warning; unmount clears the marker. Probe attempt 2 exited 0, in ai/surface-review-20260913/impl_fresco/probe-impl_fresco-2.log and .exit. Attempt 1 established those assertions but exited 1 because the harness removed its temporary window before a queued React scheduler task finished; attempt 2 retained the process-local host until normal process exit. Both roots were unmounted and no server persisted. This proves React's host premise, not a compiled Fresco/browser reproduction. A repair must earn the public red/green witness.

Deduplication and references

Revalidated and split finding 1 from prior aggregate rf2-fzbj.4; that aggregate has two independent defects and is not a substitute for this dedicated issue. Its newest three tracker history entries carry no correction or dismissal. Current live tracker searches and current exported issue descriptions found no dedicated open issue covering this path. Closed rf2-kuky.59/PR #9469 fixed adapter-independent draining of roots already in active-roots; its latest closure was read, and this failure happens before entry into that now-correct set. Do not reopen or redo that completed repair. No source changes or build were performed; parent rf2-gwye coordinates tracker durability.
notes:
=== REMEDIATED (worker fresco-a, 2026-09-13) — PR #9764 ===

VERDICT: finding CONFIRMED at tip and FIXED.

Re-verified at trunk 2d618296e8 (the review ran against 1c9ff9697b / 9e8ca97376).
`impl/mount.cljs` `root!` still called `react-dom-client/createRoot` and only then
`render!`, and `render!` evaluates `(tree handle hiccup)` — i.e. the codec's
`root-element` -> `as-element` -> `expand-seq`, which forces a lazy child seq —
INSIDE the `flushSync` callback. So an ordinary `(map fmt rows)` whose formatter
throws left `root!` after React had marked the container and before the handle
reached `mount-client-root!`: no `track-active-root!`, no publication into the
public handle, so neither `h/unmount!` nor `drain-active-roots!` could ever reach
that Root.

THE FIX (implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/mount.cljs, `root!`):
lower the initial element BEFORE `createRoot` — the order `hydrate-root!` already
had — so a failed construction allocates nothing at all. `root!` then calls
`render!`'s one line (`flushSync` + `.render`) with the already-built element
rather than `render!` itself, because `render!` would lower the tree a second
time and lowering is where the caller's code runs. Root options, the successful
update path, the opaque public handle and the active-set liveness rule are
untouched.

THE WITNESS (new, W6 in
implementation/fresco/test/re_frame/fresco/public_root_lifecycle_dom_cljs_test.cljs):
`a-failed-first-render-leaves-no-root-on-the-callers-container` drives
`h/client-root` + `h/render!` with `[:ul (map (fn [_] (throw boom)) [1])]`, and
asserts the caller's own exception object comes back, that the container is
UNOWNED afterwards, that `h/unmount!` is then safe, that a corrected render
through the SAME handle paints with NO duplicate-createRoot warning on the
console, and that the final `h/unmount!` releases it once.

Ownership is read through React's own container mark (`__reactContainer$<key>`,
written inside `createRoot` before any render, blanked by `root.unmount()`),
because the DOM cannot discriminate: a root that never rendered leaves the
container as empty as one that was never created. The mark is read only with a
two-direction CONTROL on a live mount standing beside it (unowned -> owned ->
unowned), so a React that renamed or stopped writing it reds the control instead
of quietly greening the row. The premise was re-measured against the installed
React 19.3.0 in a process-local probe: fresh container unowned, marked by
`createRoot` ALONE and enumerable through `Object.keys`, a repeated `createRoot`
warns, and `unmount()` blanks the mark.

RED/GREEN CONTROL: the browser lane run against the pre-fix source with these tests in place (the tree of PR #9764's test-only commit 8c2de2137a) failed on exactly the expected assertions and no others, captured exit 1; the restored fix ran green, captured exit 0, 1097 tests / 5999 assertions / 0 failures. The restore was verified by blob hash: git hash-object in its default form reproduced the committed blob for both source files, and git diff --quiet HEAD exited 0 as a second instrument.

SKIPPED, with reasons (stance: fix + regression + nothing else):
- No catch/unmount/rethrow around the `.render` call itself. The bead offers it
  as the alternative repair, not as an addition; lowering first removes the
  finding's whole window, and a throw out of `.render` is a component-body error
  React owns on its own path (the bead says so in terms). Adding a `.unmount`
  inside that catch would also fire React's "synchronously unmount while
  rendering" complaint for no measured gain.
- No new input validation, lifecycle abstraction or runtime machinery, as the
  parent task asks.

## Finding 1 — P2: history routes are not reloadable through the canonical example runner

Owned defect locations:
- examples/scripts/serve-example.cjs:388-398 starts the shared static HTTP server for entry.outDir without any SPA/navigation fallback; :437-440 advertises this origin as the runnable example.
- examples/scripts/examples-staging.cjs:211-218 stages index.html, _shared, and manifest assets only. There is no fallback host page.
- examples/README.md:15-23 makes `npm run dev:example -- <build-id>` the catalogue's primary runnable path.

Supporting execution path (outside ownership, inspected to establish behavior):
- implementation/scripts/lib/local-browser-harness.cjs:653-663 passes only the static root, -a, -p, -s and -c-1 to http-server. Here -s is silent logging, not SPA serving. Neither a fallback proxy nor custom navigation handler is configured.
- The installed http-server supports 404.html or --proxy fallback, but neither is present. The synthetic-root transport probe below reproduces the installed server's actual response, rather than inferring a bug from the absence of a flag.
- examples/capabilities/routing/routing/core.cljs:43-65 registers /, /articles and /articles/:id. Its frame uses :url-bound? true and the default history strategy; the mount comments explicitly describe deep-link/refresh URL synchronization. The checked-in host has <base href="/">, which fixes subsequent asset resolution only after a host document is actually served.
- RealWorld has the same exposure after navigation to /realworld/* or /realworld-resources/*; its history base path is owned by each routing.cljs. This finding does not request changing those route contracts.

User trigger / expected versus actual:
1. From implementation/, run `npm run dev:example -- examples/routing` and open the printed root URL after the first build.
2. Navigate in the app to an article, then refresh; equivalently open `<printed-origin>/articles/intro` directly.
3. Expected: receive the example host page, load main.js, and let the existing URL-bound router show the article.
4. Actual: the static server looks for an on-disk articles/intro file under out/examples/routing, finds none, and sends its 404 response. The application cannot boot, so its otherwise-correct URL synchronization never runs.

Impact: ordinary refresh, bookmarks, copied links and direct entry fail for history-routed catalogue apps launched by the advertised one-command developer path. This is a developer-serving defect, not a framework router defect. Root boot and in-app history navigation can both work, which is why compiling and fetching only index.html/main.js/stylesheets does not witness it.

## Confirmed transport witness

Ran Node against the already-installed http-server package, using only synthetic index.html/main.js under ignored `ai/surface-review-20260912/examples-support-http-probe-2`, loopback 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port, and the same static-root/cache configuration selected by the shared harness. Every request explicitly sent `Accept: text/html`, so this is not curl's default */* ambiguity. No framework server or compiler was started.

Observed:
- GET / => 200, synthetic host body present.
- GET /articles/intro => 404, host body absent.
- GET /profile/bob/favorites => 404, host body absent.
- GET /main.js => 200, generated-asset control reachable.
- GET /missing.js => 404, missing-asset control.
- closed=true; captured probe process exit=0.

Minimal equivalent probe, after creating a scratch directory containing a synthetic index.html and main.js (run from implementation/ so require resolves):
```js
const http = require('http');
const srv = require('http-server').createServer({root: scratchRoot, cache: -1});
srv.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
  const port = srv.server.address().port;
  http.get({hostname: '127.0.0.1', port, path: '/articles/intro',
            agent: false, headers: {Accept: 'text/html'}}, res => {
    console.log(res.statusCode); // 404
    res.resume();
    res.on('end', () => srv.server.close());
  });
});
```
The executed probe used a five-second ceiling, requested all five controls, closed all connections, and awaited the underlying server's close callback. Attempt 1 already measured the same responses but its cleanup receipt was invalid: http-server's wrapper close() ignores callback arguments, so the probe's own deadline fired and returned exit 1. Attempt 2 corrected the probe to srv.server.close(callback) and completed exit 0. Neither process remains running. This was probe cleanup, not a claimed production defect.

## Precise repair recommendation and acceptance criteria

Add an explicit navigation-fallback option at the existing local-server startup seam and enable it for serve-example. For an HTML document navigation whose path has no physical file, serve that selected example's staged index.html, leaving the application router to resolve the URL. Keep the same clean-stage boundary, selected output root, compiler process, ownership-token handshake, free-port selection and cleanup. Do not introduce a new build catalogue or per-example browser matrix.

The distinction between document navigation and asset fetches is necessary: a blanket fallback that returns index.html with status 200 for missing /main.js would make waitForFirstBuild accept HTML as a compiled bundle and resurrect rf2-qwy3. Missing CSS/JS/JSON fixture requests must likewise remain missing rather than masquerading as successful HTML.

Acceptance:
1. A focused synthetic-host HTTP test using the actual server path receives the host document on a direct HTML navigation to /articles/intro, with successful navigation status, while / and real main.js still serve normally.
2. In one real examples/routing launch, navigate to an article, refresh, and open the same deep URL in a fresh tab; the route and assets load correctly each time. A representative RealWorld prefixed URL also gets the selected host page.
3. Before a watch child publishes main.js, its HTTP request still does not return a successful fallback HTML body and no live-build banner appears. A missing API JSON fixture remains a failing request.
4. Root ownership/readiness checks, explicit-port conflict rejection, --no-watch compilation failure, watcher failure and child teardown retain their existing behavior.
5. Put regression coverage in the existing implementation/scripts support-test home; no *.spec.cjs under examples/ and no production API or example model changes.

## Other review coverage and measured results

Inspected the manifest-derived standalone build/source/output selection, clean-stage path guard, per-example asset source mapping (TodoMVC npm CSS, managed HTTP fixture, both RealWorld avatars), shared-tree copying, directory-walk/read failures, port parsing/probing, watch/compile first-build lifecycle, Story testbed rosters and exit propagation, play discovery/vacuity/terminal-state decisions, browser error verdicts, and shared navigation/assertion helpers. Read the catalogue/TESTING/shared-assets documentation against the neighboring package scripts, shadow configuration, tests and example route hosts. Reviewed shared CSS geometry/tokens/focus and SVG source; the PNG was checked by the existing validator, not rendered visually.

Focused process-local probes, all exit 0 in their successful final runs:
- Actual asset scanner API: 33 host pages, 0 asset errors, 0 shared-tree errors. Injected removal of counter/index.html's main.js script via readFileSync override produced the expected 'no live <script src>' error naming that exact page. No source file was modified for this negative control.
- Boundary scanner API: 74 stock-Reagent source files, 0 boundary errors; synthetic reagent2 require was detected.
- Standalone manifest resolution: 34 entries; all host paths exist and all output paths are strictly under implementation/out/examples. This is inventory/staging coverage, not 34 runtime launches.
- Existing PNG validator: ok=true, width=1200, height=630 for og.png.
- Both explicit-port resolvers reject a port held by a bounded process-local loopback listener; out-of-range/non-numeric explicit values reject. Listener closed before completion.
- First-build wait resolves only after the third non-empty synthetic publication; aborted wait returns false; code-0 watcher exit before readiness is terminal; nonzero watcher result grades failure.
- Story empty discovery rejects; a pageerror grades failure even when there are no play mismatches; cannot-run is terminal.

## Known history / duplicate distinctions

- rf2-rxja is CLOSED / WITHDRAWN AS NOT A DEFECT. Its original 404 report concerned shadow-cljs dev-http, which already serves fallback HTML when Accept permits HTML; its default curl */* requests measured a different behavior. Read both description and close_reason. The present finding concerns http-server through dev:example, not shadow-cljs, and the executed requests explicitly accept text/html. Its withdrawal does not refute this witness.
- rf2-qwy3 is closed after fixing first-build advertisement and code-0 watcher exit before readiness (latest serve-example source commits c794aa7a0c / faaf666d1b). The current checks were inspected and exercised. This bead concerns route-document serving after launch, not a recurrence of the already-fixed initial-build lifecycle defect.
- rf2-iacw2 and rf2-ujdn0 corrected launch documentation and verified root/index/main.js/stylesheet serving; they did not verify refresh at a history route. Preserve those canonical dev:example recipes and repair the server they invoke.
- rf2-y1kbf guards the host's bootstrap-script reference; its negative control still rejects. A correct host reference cannot cause a missing route document to be served.
- rf2-8cevm makes absence of per-example specs intentional. That absence is not a finding and this recommendation preserves it.
Targeted all-status tracker searches for serve-example/dev:example/staging/SPA/fallback, plus readback of the relevant source-linked beads, found no current bead owning this http-server deep-navigation defect.

## Validation limits / exclusions

No production edits, builds, dependency installs, framework-server startup, commits, checkout, rebase or push were performed. No broad test gate was run for a read-only review. Scanner results above are direct API probes with explicit source roots and injected negative controls, not a claim of a passing CI suite. No full Playwright example launch or end-to-end Story deck execution was performed. Browser layout, font rendering, later compiler reload timing, all alternate asset-parser syntaxes and arbitrary filesystem/junction failure modes were not exhaustively tested. They remain unverified, not additional defects. Parent owns tracker checkpoint/push.

Verdict: leave this bead OPEN for the single P2 serving repair. No other support-slice follow-up is warranted from this review.

title: surface-review(ssr-ring): bound Node response-body reads and release timed-out request frames
description:
Recommendation: enforce the Node renderer's HTTP deadline through complete response-body consumption, cancel the live exchange on expiry, and let the existing render-failure projection release the Ring request frame. This focused review confirms one P2 defect. Keep this task OPEN until that repair and its focused public-handler regression land. No new public timeout knob or streaming thread pool is needed.

## Scope and baseline

Owned slice: impl_ssr_ring, exactly implementation/ssr-ring/** (36 tracked paths, enumerated below).
Revision reviewed: 1c9ff9697b0fa3a018c7a4371e02983ad2e79b2f.
SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2.
WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review).

The root made a beads-only checkpoint while this review ran (HEAD became 5b89378c457e9997d7eff69b7dec56eec4e5307c). A final git diff against the stated baseline for implementation/ssr-ring returned no paths: the owned source under review stayed unchanged. No production/test source edits, builds, dependency installs, commits, rebase, checkout, or pushes were performed by this worker. Root owns tracker durability. The only writes were unique ignored probe/evidence/body files and this one new bead.

Coverage: inspected every production namespace in this slice: public synchronous handler/middleware and streaming facade; frame setup and exact-incarnation teardown; request-derived initial events; redirect and projected-error classification; renderer/head/payload/shell ordering; header case folding, multi-values, Content-Type override, Content-Length stripping, cookie serialization and attribute validation; payload projection's explicit frame target and separate client wire id; streaming request-thread shell preparation, daemon pipe writer, FIFO/nested continuations, failed-boundary propagation, final payload and catch/finally cleanup; Node renderer construction, request state serialization, HTTP transport, deadline/refusal/build-skew classification. Inspected deps.edn's production dependencies and default/slow/crossing test lane split. Read relevant deadline, renderer-seam, materializer, writer/disconnect and final-payload regression sections and inventoried the remaining tests and fixtures.

Limits: no full suite or broad gate, shared compilation, browser hydration, Node sidecar startup, Jetty/http-kit/Aleph deployment, real network-disconnect test, stress/concurrency run, cold dependency resolution, package publication, or exhaustive execution of all test files. The actual Node transport was exercised against a bounded ephemeral loopback HTTP peer, explicitly authorized by the root; its listener/exchanges/futures were closed in finally. The streamed-response close probe directly closed the Ring InputStream in process. It verifies the adapter's pipe/teardown path, not a host's socket-to-body-close integration. Neighboring SSR/HTTP code was followed only as a contract/dependency; the SSR and HTTP review beads retain their own ownership.

## Finding 1 — P2: the Node renderer's HTTP deadline does not bound response-body reads

Owned sources:
- implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/node.clj:236-241 derives the advertised HTTP budget as timeout-ms + admission-ms + wire-margin-ms.
- node.clj:271-278 applies it only with HttpRequest.Builder.timeout.
- node.clj:348-361, especially 353, blocks in HttpClient.send with BodyHandlers.ofString; there is no independent deadline through complete body consumption. The catch at 359 can classify a JDK timeout only when one is delivered.
- node.clj:418-426 calls that blocking transport from the actual renderer closure.
- implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/pipeline.clj:632-643 invokes the renderer inside the live request-frame scope before assembling the document.
- implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring.clj:299-338 owns the synchronous request and reaches its frame-destroy finally only after the renderer returns or throws.

Contract: node.clj:35-48 promises an explicit HTTP timeout including a wire margin, separate from the sidecar render deadline. The original crossing contract rf2-8arzr.4 S5/S6 also names read timeout as a transport failure that must throw at the live render call site and project to a fail-closed 5xx. This finding concerns completion of that HTTP exchange, not an overall application-handler budget or interruption of arbitrary caller code.

Trigger: a configured Node endpoint (or an intermediary/remote transport) answers HTTP 200 promptly with the expected x-rf-ssr-build header and begins its body, then stalls before completing the body. The sidecar render deadline is no substitute for a JVM wire/read deadline after headers have arrived. A healthy in-process fake returning a completed body would not expose this case.

Executed public-path reproducer:
1. Load the actual current re-frame.core, re-frame.ssr, re-frame.ssr.ring and re-frame.ssr.ring.node namespaces; initialize rf with ssr/adapter. No production function was redefined or replaced.
2. Start an ephemeral loopback HttpServer whose /render peer consumes the POST, returns x-rf-ssr-build: review-build and Content-Length: 2, writes/flushed byte A, then waits on a release latch before byte B. The latch has a finite 4-second safety backstop and the server/exchange is closed in finally.
3. Construct node/renderer with {:entry "review/root", :build-id "review-build", :timeout-ms 100, :admission-ms 0, :render-state {:app-db [:review/value]}} and the peer endpoint. The real computed HTTP budget is 100 + 0 + 500 = 600 ms.
4. Pass that renderer into the real ring/ssr-handler with {:initial-events [], :payload [:review/value]}. A thin observation wrapper records the renderer's frame-id and catches/rethrows its unchanged exception; it does not change transport behavior. Invoke the handler with a normal GET Ring request in a disposable future.
5. After observing the peer's first body byte, wait another 1500 ms for the handler. Result: pending=true at 1622.256 ms total; request-frame-live=true; no error id. The handler has exceeded its 600 ms HTTP budget while retaining its request frame.
6. Release byte B. The same handler returns status 200 with AB in its generated document; only then is request-frame-live=false. This is success after the stated deadline, not just a slow error path.
7. Control: delay the peer BEFORE headers with the same renderer options and same 600 ms budget. The actual handler returns projected status 500 at 608.8762 ms, with :rf.error/ssr-node-deadline and the frame already absent. Releasing the peer afterwards does not turn this into success.

Expected: expiry of the derived HTTP deadline before the entire body is read cancels the exchange, throws the existing :rf.error/ssr-node-deadline with :observed-by :jvm, produces the existing projected non-200 error response without partial success HTML/hydration state, and reaches exact-frame teardown promptly.
Actual: on installed JDK 21.0.10 the HttpRequest timeout protects the pre-header phase but does not bound this BodyHandlers.ofString response-body wait. A stalled peer can keep the synchronous Ring request and frame live indefinitely; if it eventually finishes, the renderer returns success after the budget.
Impact: Node-backed SSR can exhaust host request concurrency and retain per-request state despite the explicit timeout that operators rely on. The failure is possible with valid renderer configuration and an ordinary stalled/trickling upstream response. It is independent of managed HTTP request IDs and applies even though the Node renderer correctly uses one shared HttpClient.

Precise repair: enforce the already-derived deadline across completion of the full response/body future, with cancellation reaching the underlying JDK exchange. One local approach is sendAsync with the same body handler, a bounded wait using the remaining deadline, and cancel(true) on expiry/interruption; preserve the one-client-per-renderer model. Translate expiry through throw-deadline! opts :jvm so existing projection and finally behavior do the rest. Clear any timer/completion resources on success, refusal, I/O failure and interruption. title: surface-review(machines-viz): repair parallel containment and function-delay sharing
description:
Fix parallel-region containment in the xyflow projection and make function-valued :after delays shareable without carrying executable values. This focused read-only review confirms two P2 correctness defects. Keep this bead OPEN until both are repaired; the existing tests currently encode the first defect and omit the second supported grammar arm.

## Scope and baseline

Owned slice: tools_machines_viz — exactly tools/machines-viz/** (74 tracked paths in ai/surface-review-20260912/partition.json).
Revision reviewed: 1c9ff9697b0fa3a018c7a4371e02983ad2e79b2f.
SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2.
WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review).
No production edits, builds, dependency installs, server startup, or git mutations were performed. Root owns the durable checkpoint/push.

Coverage: inspected the grammar/desugaring boundary; semantic node/edge generation and stable IDs; live snapshot highlights and fired/blocked projection; ELK children and coordinate extraction; MachineChart parse/layout caches, stale-settle guard, measurement and fit callbacks; React/UIx adapters; overlay anchor/scaffold lifecycle; share sanitization/validation, viewer entry, image/export seams; README/API and package/test-lane declarations. Read focused projection, stale-settle, and share regressions. Executed targeted process-local probes against current source and cached dependencies, detailed below.

Exclusions: no full browser rendering or DOM interaction suite, screenshot comparison, canvas/clipboard operation, shared compilation, broad test gate, deployment/cold package resolution, exhaustive SCXML/Mermaid grammar corpus, or live Xray/Story session. Neighboring machines specification and dependency implementation were read only as contracts/oracles. Lack of a test alone was not treated as a defect.

## Finding 1 — P2: parallel regions lose their root-container parent in xyflow

Source: tools/machines-viz/src/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/chart/projection.cljc:1604-1606. Supporting path: chart/layout.cljc:1329-1340 wraps every parentless node, including each region, in root-container-id; projection.cljc:927-1008 builds the corresponding nested ELK children; chart.cljs:478-485 preserves each ELK node's parent-relative x/y. Existing contrary test: tools/machines-viz/test/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/chart/projection_cljs_test.cljc:393-405 explicitly asserts that the region container has no parentId or extent.

Trigger/reproducer (valid ordinary parallel machine):

```clojure
(def d
  {:type :parallel
   :regions {:a {:initial :idle
                 :states {:idle {:on {:go :done}}
                          :done {:final? true}}}
             :b {:initial :idle :states {:idle {}}}}})
(def parsed (layout/project-definition d))
;; Each region in parsed has :parent-id layout/root-container-id.
;; Each corresponding (projection/xyflow-graph parsed positions {}) node
;; has NO :parentId because the guard excludes region?.
```

Expected: the region is a child of the named root frame, and xyflow's absolute position equals the parent-relative ELK position plus the frame origin. Its descendants and ELK's ROOT-coordinate routes agree.
Actual: the (not region?) guard strips only these parent links. xyflow treats the region position as absolute, while its descendants inherit that incorrectly placed region. ELK's edge routes remain in the correct absolute frame.

Executed evidence: Babashka loaded the actual current layout/projection CLJC source. A Node process then ran cached elkjs with the actual default-elk-options map read from chart.cljs plus INCLUDE_CHILDREN, actual ->elk-children / ->elk-edges outputs, and the installed @xyflow/system adoptUserNodes function. Only process-local graph objects were changed. Results at the default layout:

- root frame: ELK absolute (12,12), xyflow absolute (12,12).
- region__a: ELK absolute (38,52), xyflow absolute (26,40), parentId absent.
- region__b: ELK absolute (250,118), xyflow absolute (238,106), parentId absent.
- region__a__idle: ELK absolute (64,92), xyflow absolute (52,80).
- region__a__done: ELK absolute (64,224), xyflow absolute (52,212).
- region__b__idle: ELK absolute (276,158), xyflow absolute (264,146).

The probe completed exit 0 and established a (-12,-12) mismatch throughout the region subtrees; this is an observed coordinate defect, not a screenshot claim. A second direct projection probe with a synthetic frame origin (100,200) independently showed the same missing-parent mechanism.

Impact: every default parallel chart places regions and their contents outside the intended frame coordinate system. Routed transition geometry and rendered node boxes disagree, undermining the chart's main topology-reading surface. The offset is the frame origin, not a fixed correction to bake into region positions.

Repair: propagate an existing :parent-id to :parentId for region containers just as for other nodes; preserve parent-first ordering and the existing parent-relative positions. Update the stale 'region container is not nested' regression instead of retaining its pre-root-container assumption. Check the opt-in post-ELK region transform against the restored parent relationship, without broad layout redesign.

Acceptance:
- A real parsed parallel graph places every region under layout/root-container-id in both ELK and xyflow.
- Given a nonzero frame origin, adopting projected nodes through xyflow yields the same absolute positions as summing the ELK ancestry for region containers, leaves, event nodes, and initial markers.
- A focused rendered parallel fixture confirms node/edge alignment and that the named frame encloses the graph, including a context band; exercise :tb and the existing :auto path.
- Flat and nested-compound containment continues to work; all parents precede their children.

History: rf2-q129z8 introduced the root frame at 0d543b1b04224f69891a78e297355fa738217815. Its historical close_reason, read by exact issue identity from that revision's .beads/issues.jsonl, says validation covered flat door and compound hvac/media nesting; this missing parallel case survives in today's test assertion. The old ID is absent from the current live tracker. This finding is distinct from closed rf2-x19xi, whose implemented cross-topology stale-settle equality guard was inspected and whose existing regression was read.

## Finding 2 — P2: valid function-valued :after keys survive share sanitization and fail Transit encoding

Source: tools/machines-viz/src/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/share.cljs:245-260, especially :else [k (sanitise-definition v)] at line 260. The unsupported function reaches the plain transit/write at share.cljs:695-696. The accepted grammar arm is tools/machines-viz/src/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/grammar.cljc:712-717; the public function-valued delay is specified at spec/005-StateMachines.md:2365. The advertised share guarantee is tools/machines-viz/spec/API.md:1770-1785: any inline function becomes an opaque label and the resulting topology contains no functions.

Trigger/reproducer:

```clojure
(def delay-fn (fn [_ctx] 1000))
(def d {:initial :idle
        :states {:idle {:after {delay-fn :done}}
                 :done {}}})
(share/encode-share-url {:machine-id :demo :definition d}
                       {:host "/viewer.html"})
```

Expected: a viewer-safe share link preserving the delayed transition as an inert, labeled topology edge, without evaluating or serializing the delay function.
Actual: sanitise-definition recursively visits map VALUES but returns k unchanged. An :after delay is a map KEY, so the function survives. The canonical grammar explicitly accepts fn? delay keys, allowing validation to pass; canonicalise also preserves the key. Transit then receives an executable function with no write handler and encoding throws rather than returning a link.

Executed evidence: the four required pure sanitization forms (source-debug-keys, fn-label-marker, fn-name-label, sanitise-definition) were read from the current share.cljs and evaluated unchanged in isolated Babashka/JVM processes. The current grammar CLJC was required from its absolute source root. For the function-delay definition, original-valid=true, sanitized-valid=true, and the sanitized :after key was identical to the original function. A JVM Transit check using already-cached transit-clj/transit-java then produced:

```
:literal  :valid true :fn-key false :transit :ok
:fn-delay :valid true :fn-key true  :transit :error
cause: java.lang.Exception: Not supported: class user$eval581$fn__582
```

Both probe processes completed exit 0; the expected writer exception was caught and reported. The literal-delay control serialized successfully. The CLJS transit-js dependency source was also inspected: its standard handler table has no Function handler and its writer's fallback throws Cannot write <constructor name>. The full CLJS encode-share-url entry was NOT executed; the exact unchanged sanitization/grammar path and JVM writer failure were executed, while the final CLJS writer failure is established by the inspected call and handler path. No outdated compiled application bundle was used as current-source evidence.

Impact: the advertised share workflow fails for a valid, explicitly supported runtime machine shape, including local-machine-data-derived timeouts. This is normal API use, not malformed-input hardening.

Repair: make share sanitization grammar-aware for :after delay keys. Convert function-valued delays to inert, serializable, distinctly labeled viewer representations accepted by the share/projector grammar, preserving every target/candidate. Do not call delay functions to obtain values: that would run caller code and depend on a live snapshot. Preserve normal keyword state/event/region keys and the earlier :fn-topology-key fix. Keep multiple anonymous function delay keys distinct so the rewrite cannot silently merge their transitions.

Acceptance:
- In the actual CLJS share test lane, encode/decode the reproducer and render/project its decoded definition successfully.
- The payload contains no live functions in either keys or values; the delay function is never invoked.
- Literal and subscription-vector :after keys retain current behavior.
- A definition with two distinct anonymous fn delay keys retains both transition branches after round trip.
- Existing named/inline guard/action sanitization and topology entries named :fn still pass.

History: rf2-m285a's historical closed record (read by exact identity from 0e266e89fa:.beads/issues.jsonl) documents the original structural share sanitizer. rf2-07gg7h and fix commit 0e266e89fa63980fbb637d17a3f71a00292b4908 corrected deletion of ordinary topology entries named :fn. Neither covered executable delay keys. These historical IDs are absent from the current live tracker, so their present status is not inferred from an old snapshot. Current all-status tracker searches found no duplicate for either finding.

## Validation limits and follow-up posture

Confirmed findings: 2, both P2. No additional speculative risks are promoted to remediation. Lifecycle callback races within one layout key, browser-only overlay alignment under user pan/zoom, image rasterization, and exhaustive importer semantics were not established as defects in this bounded review. The existing cross-topology stale-settle fix was not reported again. Focused acceptance tests above are the remaining implementation work; this review does not claim the full suites passed.

title: Incomplete: revived column-width isolation test leaves instance B storage behind
description:
Merged-PR audit #9688, merge 5fc27ca2365328dc26d10a716860ce75653217ce (2026-09-11T10:27:01Z), source rf2-r51p. The revived browser test custom-storage-key-isolates-per-instance in tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/views/resizable_table_persistence_dom_cljs_test.cljs:92-111 assumes story.testbed.b.column-widths is empty at line106, then writes {:t2 {:b 200}} to it at line108, switches back to A, and never clears B. The fixture at53-60 clears only the currently selected key and then selects the default; it cannot clear B after this row ends on A. The shared runtime fixture runs post-reset only as initialization and does not clear browser localStorage in finalization. Production rt/clear! removes only get-storage-key.

A second invocation on the same browser origin therefore reaches line106 with the prior B value and fails an isolation assertion even though production isolation is correct. This is a deterministic source-level state trace, not an executed browser rerun. It matters for repeated local/browser-watch runs and for this test leaving its own persistent state behind. The old row was unreachable in both lanes; moving it into the browser makes the latent cleanup omission live. No exact open Bead records this storage-key cleanup defect; rf2-r51p records lane-dead assertions and its remaining files, a different correction.

Make this row own both test keys: establish their empty initial state, clear both in finally, and restore the default key even if setup/body throws. Follow the nearby filters persistence isolation test cleanup pattern, with guaranteed restoration. Keep the positive A round-trip and cross-instance assertions unchanged. No general fixture redesign is needed.
acceptance_criteria: Run the isolation row twice against the same browser localStorage origin; both runs pass without manually clearing storage. After either success or an injected body exception, both test keys are removed and the storage-key override is reset. Preserve the original A/B isolation assertions and all other revived cases.
close_reason:
DONE — PR #9693 merged (test(xray): let the column-width isolation row own both storage keys),
87/87 at head 322a1e92bf, rebased onto main at 163fb6410a. One file, 55 insertions / 15 deletions.

Premise held in every clause and was re-checked at source: `rt/clear!` removes only
`(get-storage-key)`; the fixture's `:post-reset` is initialisation-only and clears just the
currently-selected key; the row ended on instance A leaving `story.testbed.b.column-widths` behind.

Reproduced, which is the part worth keeping:

* The canonical runner calls `browser.newContext()` — an EPHEMERAL context — so `npm run
  test:browser` and CI start from an empty origin and NEVER see this. Driving `out/browser-test`
  with ONE context and two loads reproduced it: pre-fix 11 failures then 12, post-fix 11 then 11.
  The extra failure was exactly the `(= {} (rt/load))` line in
  `custom-storage-key-isolates-per-instance`.
* So the bead's "second invocation" mechanism is right, and CI was never exposed and still is not.
  The leak could only bite `browser-watch` and repeated hand-runs against a persistent profile.
* Injected-exception witness: a planted throw after the B write gave `11 failures, 1 errors` naming
  the row, and localStorage afterwards carried NEITHER test key — so the runtime observed the plant.
  Restore verified by blob hash against the committed object plus `git diff --quiet HEAD`.

Deliberately NOT fixed, recorded so it is not re-discovered as new: `hydrate-lifts-persisted-widths`
(last row in the namespace) leaves `re-frame2.xray.column-widths.v1` in storage at end-of-namespace,
for the same initialisation-only-fixture reason. It causes no cross-run red, because the next run's
`:post-reset` clears the default key first. Out of this bead's scope; file it if the persistent-profile
lane ever becomes a gate.

title: Incomplete: acceptance C4 never targets an inspected application
description:
Merged-PR audit #9669, merge b2ac2f879ffd59dd052225b70de8fd4bd2fcb5a2 (2026-09-11T07:27:47Z), source rf2-k97c.3. This concerns the new acceptance instrument, not a newly observed production defect. The parent criterion is tool-local state separate from the app, WITH COMMANDS TARGETING THE INTENDED APP FRAME. acceptance/test_helpers/criteria.cljs:595-683 exercises only :rf.xray.static/select-tab in xray-frame. Its app-frame is asserted untouched and other-frame holds another tool tab. This is useful proof of tool-local dispatch capture, but no tool-issued command ever targets either inspected application. A regression routing every app-directed Xray command to the wrong app frame therefore leaves this C4 green. Changing mount-xray!'s surface vector when the root swap lands cannot add that missing action.

Extend the shared C4 body with one existing app-directed Xray operation through its real UI/dispatch path, with two inspected application frames seeded differently. Verify the selected app receives the intended effect, the other app is unchanged, and tool-local state remains in :rf/xray. Keep the current tab case. If the action is not available on the staged Static subject, wire that bounded case when the harness moves to the shipped shell; do not represent the current row as full criterion-4 coverage meanwhile. No new product command or general testing framework is needed.
acceptance_criteria: The shared browser acceptance body runs an existing app-directed Xray command in both adapter arms and proves the selected application changes while a distinct unselected application does not. A disabled or misrouted app command makes the case fail. Existing tool-tab isolation remains covered; documentation distinguishes the staged Static coverage from the complete criterion until this case is wired.
notes:
=== IMPLEMENTED 2026-09-11, PR #9684, branch worker/acccrit-a (with rf2-kay8, one file, one dispatch). ===

Worker worktree guard RAN and exited 0. Merge base d1c08b7c86, rebased onto origin/main
(16 commits, none touching tools/xray/test/.../acceptance/**) before marking ready.

## THE PREMISE HOLDS, AND THE FALLBACK BRANCH IS THE OUTCOME

Confirmed at tip: the shared C4 body issues only `:rf.xray.static/select-tab` — into the
xray frame via the tab click, and into the deaf tool frame before the mount. `app-frame`
is only ever ASSERTED UNTOUCHED; nothing is ever commanded into it. The bead is right.

THE APP-DIRECTED OPERATION THIS BEAD ASKS FOR DOES NOT EXIST ON THE STAGED STATIC
SUBJECT, so this takes the fallback the bead's own description names in its last
sentences, and the acceptance criteria's own final clause ("documentation distinguishes
the staged Static coverage from the complete criterion until this case is wired").

MEASURED over `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/static/**`: the ONLY `{:frame ...}`
DISPATCH option in the whole Static tree is `defaults/default-frame-id`, which IS the
Xray frame (the four sites are in `static/machines/instances_jump.cljs`). The `{:frame
...}` occurrences in `static/schemas/panel.cljs` are cross-frame READS
(`rf.schemas/app-schemas`), not commands. POSITIVE CONTROL for that census, so the zero
is absence rather than a broken instrument: the Dynamic `panels/` tree carries 64
`{:frame` sites and 63 `target-frame` references against Static's 2, and both of
Static's are prose inside docstrings.

THE ABSENCE IS DELIBERATE, WHICH IS WHY NO PRODUCT COMMAND WAS ADDED.
`static/routes/simulate_nav.cljs` states the posture in terms — "Xray is a lens, not a
remote control" — and `static/machines/sim.cljs` clones the machine definition into

affordances, the `(fn [ev] (rf/dispatch ev {:frame frame}))` closures, all live on the
DYNAMIC side, whose shell is still an `rf/reg-view` painted through the installed
adapter and is a later slice. No new product command and no testing framework was built.

## WHAT LANDED

The implementation-governing conclusion is in the TRACKED FILE, not only here: C4's own
docstring and the namespace header of
`tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/acceptance/test_helpers/criteria.cljs` now state

WHAT THE ROW COULD GAIN, IT GAINED. A SECOND inspected application (`second-app-frame`,

so the claim is about applications in the plural — one untouched application is

## THE NEW ASSERTIONS ARE PROVEN TO BITE

file to the committed blob exactly.

## STATUS

Left OPEN deliberately: the PR is not merged, and closing a bead ahead of its merge
would be premature. Captured gate exits and the full measurement are in PR #9684's
`## Quality gates` section.

title: DIAGNOSE: xray-feature-gate full sweep fails '20-event large value elision load' on the App-db panel, and no nightly has run since it landed
description:
A LIVE REGRESSION IS SITTING ON TRUNK THAT NO CI RUN HAS SEEN YET, AND TONIGHT'S NIGHTLY WILL
FIND IT. This bead is DIAGNOSIS ONLY — locate the cause and FILE the fix; do not fix it here.

=== THE FAILURE (reported by the static6-a worker, measured in ITS tree — inference for you) ===

`npm run test:xray-feature-gate`, FULL sweep (not the PR-smoke tier), fails the scenario
`20-event large value elision load` on the selector `[data-testid="rf-xray-app-db-diff"]` — the
App-db panel that landed as increment 5 of rf2-k97c.3.

The worker measured it three ways and reports:
  * with its own two source files reverted to the merge base, the sweep gives the IDENTICAL
    result — so it is not static6's change;
  * it still fails on the final base — so it is not a stale-tree artefact;
  * **rf2-d2aj's landing (`ba26dd1aa7`) did NOT fix it**, which is worth stating because that PR
    rewrote this very panel's mount identity an hour earlier and is the obvious suspect.
  * `PASS static mode chrome and chord` throughout, so the Static shell mounts fine — the failure
    is specific.

**TREAT ALL OF THAT AS A CLAIM.** It was measured in another worktree, on another branch, by a
worker whose slice was elsewhere. Reproduce it in yours before you diagnose anything.

=== WHAT THE MAYOR VERIFIED, AND THIS PART IS FACT ===

**No run of `expensive-tests.yml` has happened since increment 5 landed.** Increment 5
(`f05040ae9b`, the App-db and Graph panels) landed 2026-09-10 13:08 AUSEST = 03:08 UTC. The run
listing at the time of filing:

    2026-09-10T01:34  workflow_dispatch  completed/success
    2026-09-10T01:14  workflow_dispatch  completed/cancelled
    2026-09-09T15:25  schedule           completed/success
    ... every earlier run older still

The most recent run of ANY kind predates the landing by ninety minutes, and the last SCHEDULED one
predates it by twelve hours. So CI has genuinely not seen this, and the full sweep is nightly-tier
— the PR-smoke tier that runs per PR does not cover it, which is why increment 5 merged green and
why every PR since has too.

**The schedule fires at 15:25 UTC daily**, so this goes red tonight unless it is fixed. That is
the whole reason this is P2 rather than P3.

**AND THERE IS NO ALERT CHANNEL WIRED IN THIS REPOSITORY** — `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md` has
a standing tick that copies open nightly alerts into the tracker, and it is deliberately not owed
here because CLAUDE.md carries none of the values it needs (measured: zero occurrences of "alert"
in that file, against a live control). So a red nightly is not going to announce itself. The
method records the cost of exactly that: an alerter opened its issue on the first red night,
notified three more times across a week, and the redness was still found by hand on day seven.
**This bead IS the alert.**

=== WHY THIS IS DIAGNOSIS-ONLY, AND THE FENCE IS NOT NEGOTIABLE ===

The obvious place to look is `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/app_db_diff.cljs` and
`panels/app_db_diff_state.cljs`. **A LIVE WORKER HOLDS BOTH** (`samefrm-a`, rf2-t3fz — the
same-frame instance-isolation residual, a P2 with an open change).

**READ THEM. DO NOT EDIT THEM.** Your deliverable is a located root cause and a filed fix bead,
which is exactly what an owner who already has that file open needs in order to land the fix
inside the change that is already there. If the root cause turns out to be somewhere nobody holds
— the scenario file, the testbed, the elision logic, a selector that moved — say so, and say
whether the fix is small enough to belong on this bead after all. That is a finding, and you
should report it rather than acting on it.

The scenario roster is centrally owned by `tools/xray/testbeds/feature_matrix/scenarios.cjs`.

=== WHAT A GOOD ANSWER LOOKS LIKE ===

Not "the panel is broken". Name the mechanism: what the scenario asserts, what it actually gets,
and which change made the difference. Bisect if you must — the suspect window is narrow and every
commit in it is on trunk:

    f05040ae9b   the App-db and Graph panels migrate to Fresco boundaries (increment 5)
    ...          the increments after it
    ba26dd1aa7   rf2-d2aj, the inspector lifecycle key

**AND CHECK WHETHER IT EVER PASSED.** "A regression" is itself a claim. If the scenario was
added or last changed alongside the panel, this may be a test that has never been green on the
full sweep rather than a working thing that broke — a different defect with a different owner, and
the distinction changes who fixes it. `git log` on the scenario file settles it in one command.

=== THE GATE IS HEAVY AND FIVE OTHER WORKERS ARE LIVE ===

The full feature-matrix sweep is exactly the "heavy enough that two runs cannot coexist" shape:
it WEDGES rather than fails — no progress, no exit file, no error, from a run healthy a minute
ago. **Read the clock before killing anything on elapsed time** — ask the system for the time
rather than inferring it from how much has happened; that has failed in both directions here, one
worker killing a healthy run believing seventeen minutes had passed when it had been two.

If you detach it, poll BOTH the log and the exit-code file in a bounded loop WITHIN THE SAME TURN.
**The turn ends only once the exit file exists and its number is quoted.** A Monitor, a watch, a
subscription, a background task you expect to wake you — every one is the same strand.

**GATE THE BROWSER STEP ON THE COMPILE'S CAPTURED EXIT.** A browser lane chained behind a failed
compile SERVES THE PREVIOUS BUNDLE and returns a plausible green with its own honest exit code —
measured this session, 885 tests against stale code. That failure mode is especially dangerous
HERE, because you are trying to tell one tree's behaviour from another's.

**And quote the number you captured, never one your harness reports about the same run.** The
static6-a worker reported that its harness said "exit code 0" three times for runs whose captured
exit was 1, and the file was right every time.
close_reason:
DIAGNOSIS DELIVERED AND COMPLETE. This bead's deliverable was an explanation, not a patch; the patch is rf2-qhoj (P1), filed from this work with the site, the mechanism and the coverage gap. Closing on the diagnosis, not on a merge — there is no PR here and there was never meant to be one. Status was stale: it read in_progress with no live worker after its worker reported and was reaped.

THE MECHANISM, NAMED TO ONE TOKEN. tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/views/edn_inspector.cljs:2818 reads [mini prior 40] and must read (mini prior 40) -- inside render-leaf's :modified -> type-change? branch, the R7 'was <prior>' suffix.     f05040ae9b^ = e19cc792eb          1          1         126236              0

'feature matrix shell and panel handoff' IS a smoke scenario and it DOES click the app-db tab -- but on /counter/, where the diff is number-to-number. The branch needs a LEAF TYPE CHANGE. deliberate — `impl/collector.cljs`'s `cell-reapers`: a cell whose last reader unmounts is
given one macrotask of grace so a keyed reorder that unmounts and remounts within one turn
reuses the reaction. Measured: a synchronous read straight after `flushSync(root.unmount)`
returns ref-count 1; one macrotask later it returns 0. A synchronous assertion reports a
LEAK against a collector behaving exactly as documented. W4 polls. Anyone migrating a panel
and measuring teardown meets this first.

## THE DISPATCH QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND IT BINDS EVERY REMAINING PANEL

The template (module_view) has NO dispatch, so increment 1 left the question open. It is
answerable at source, in Fresco's own shipped code, and needs no new idiom:

  re-frame.fresco.impl.intent/with-frame is what a boundary body runs inside
  (collector/run-once calls it per render). Its docstring is normative and says three things:

  (a) it binds core's REFUSAL TIER, so an ambient (rf/subscribe ...) or (rf/dispatch ...)
      REFUSES for the extent of the body. Migrating a body's reads to rf.fresco/sub is
      therefore MANDATORY, not stylistic -- a left-behind @(rf/subscribe ...) does not
      silently read the wrong frame, it refuses.
  (b) "the refusal deletes the ambient FIND, not the carrying" -- an explicitly carried
      {:frame <id>} STILL ANSWERS.
  (c) the pure doors rf/current-frame-id and zero-arity rf/capture-frame ANSWER THE DECLARED
      FRAME, "because neither reads nor dispatches". re-frame.fresco's own ns docstring says
      the same from the other side: "The frame doors are core's ... this door duplicates
      neither."

  And re-frame.fresco/defview's docstring, section "What a value at an on-* prop may be --
  FOUR shapes", records that A PLAIN FUNCTION IS PASSED THROUGH UNTOUCHED, reaching React by
  identity.

CONSEQUENCE, and it is the good news: the rf2-nesy9 render-time frame capture these panels
already do -- (let [frame (rf/current-frame-id)] ... :on-click (fn [_] (rf/dispatch ev
{:frame frame}))) -- is EXACTLY RIGHT under a Fresco boundary and carries over unchanged.
Do not rewrite those handlers into intent vectors; both spellings are legal and the plain-fn
one is already there and already correct.

THE ONE DISPATCH SHAPE THAT DOES BREAK is reg-view's LEXICALLY INJECTED bare `dispatch` (and
bare `subscribe`) -- the class the ruling counted at 109 + 6 sites. defview "binds NO name
inside your body, so every symbol a body resolves is one you wrote", so an injected name is
simply unresolved. It fails loudly at compile, which is the good failure. Replace with

Step 1 says the widget's head use sites "each take an `as-component` bridge until its own
panel migrates". THEY CANNOT. The inspected VALUE cannot cross a Reagent props crossing.

Fresco's own `as-component` docstring says so in terms — the outward decode is SHALLOW,
"values therefore cross BY IDENTITY here, which is a fact about this decode rather than a
promise about what arrives — a Reagent parent's `[:>]` runs its own `convert-prop-value`
first, so a keyword reaches the body as its name and a map as a camelCased object. Names
round-trip across a crossing; values do not."

Increment 1's `module_view` bridge is sound BECAUSE it crosses an EMPTY props map
(`[:> Panel-component {}]`). That is not a stylistic choice that generalises; it is the
only shape that survives the crossing. This widget's entire payload is an arbitrary CLJS
value, which is precisely what the crossing destroys.

The dodges were considered and rejected. Wrapping the payload in a `#js{}` so Reagent's
`convert-prop-value` passes it through by identity works, but it leans on a Reagent
implementation detail, and — decisively — it changes the Reagent-visible hiccup, which

## THE THREE CLOSURE ATOMS, AND WHY THIS IS THE INTERESTING PART

A Fresco boundary is a real React function component and has NO form-2, so a closure
allocated in its body is allocated PER RENDER. The ResizeObserver would be rebuilt and the
projection cache discarded on every pass — and the invisible one: A REF CALLBACK MINTED PER
RENDER CHANGES IDENTITY EVERY RENDER, so React detaches and re-attaches it every time,
tearing the observer down and standing a new one up in a loop, with nothing wrong-looking
in the rendered output.

So the three moved into ONE module-level store keyed by mount-id, released together when
React calls the container `:ref` with nil. `container-ref-for` MEMOISES the ref per mount,
which is the contract rather than an optimisation. The Reagent head lost its closure atoms
too and now shares the same store and the same lifecycle.

`mount-state-count` and `mount-state-held` are test surfaces so teardown is ASSERTABLE
rather than assumed.

## A REAL FINDING FROM W2'S RED, WORTH THE NEXT WORKER'S TIME

W2's deaf control failed against a DOM reading the whole value on one line, with no
container node in it at all. NOTHING WAS BROKEN. A mount's FIRST render is depth-driven
because no width measurement has arrived; the container ref then measures, the width
reaches the slot, and the next render INLINES anything whose pr-str fits the measured
column. So a small value legitimately CHANGES SHAPE once between the mount and the first
idle moment, and any row that straddles that is asserting against a shape the widget has
already left. Anyone writing a DOM row against this widget meets this first. Use a value
too wide to inline, and settle BEFORE taking a baseline.

The diagnosis is itself evidence and the row now banks it: after settling, the width slot

one of the panel's OWN affordances, fired through the live frame -- writes Xray's app-db,
invalidates the db-backed read, and the row appears.

=== AND IT IS WRONG TWICE. INLINING IS THE RULED, TAUGHT, FIRST-CLASS SHAPE. ===

THE RULING IS HD-016 (`docs/design/fresco/decisions.md:1031`): in hiccup, a head-position view var
is a boundary child, while a plain function CALL "INLINES INTO THE ENCLOSING BOUNDARY: no boundary
of its own, and any `sub` it performs donates its read upward."

The codec's own error text names both remedies as legitimate -- "A plain function in head position
is never a silent embedding -- call it, or make it a view"
(`implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/codec.cljs:1786`). The public `sub` docstring is
explicit that inlining is supported (`implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco.cljc:433`): reads
work "inside an inlined helper", and "the edge is recorded where the read happens".

THE TWO ERRORS IN `panels.cljs:229-233`:

  (a) IT NAMES A `:rf/default` FALLBACK THAT DOES NOT EXIST. `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:1996`:
      such a plain fn's ambient subscribe/dispatch "resolves to nil and RAISES
      `:rf.error/no-frame-context` -- the operation fails fast rather than silently routing to a
      conventional default. THERE IS NO SILENT FALL-THROUGH TO `:rf/default`."
      Confirmed in the implementation: `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views/provider.cljs:247`
      `current-frame` bottoms out at nil, its docstring saying the runtime never synthesises
      `:rf/default`.

  (b) FOR A HELPER INSIDE AN ALREADY-PROVIDED TREE THE DIRECTION IS REVERSED -- HEADING IS THE
      FOOTGUN AND INLINING IS THE FIX. `current-frame` reads the context off the IN-FLIGHT
      component. A `reg-view` carries a `:contextType`; a plain `defn` does not.
        helper CALLED inside a `reg-view`/`defview` body -> the in-flight component IS the
                     boundary -> context resolves -> correct frame.
        helper HEADED -> Reagent mints a component FOR THE PLAIN FN, which has no
                     `:contextType` -> sentinel -> nil -> `:rf.error/no-frame-context`.
      `spec/006` calls this exact shape the "Plain-fn footgun".

THE DOCSTRING'S CONCLUSION IS STILL RIGHT FOR ITS OWN SITE, for a different reason: `render-panel!`
builds its provider-wrapped panel inside a PLAIN FUNCTION, so calling the panel view there would
evaluate outside any React render at all -- no in-flight component, nil, raise. It is a statement
about the MOUNT SEAM and nothing wider. THE GENERAL QUESTION IS CLOSED; stop treating it as open,
and stop carrying the warning into briefs about helpers.
