title: Xray's embed door (render-panel!/mount-shell!) still paints through the installed adapter — decide whether element-shaped panel embedding is wanted
description:
XRAY'S **EMBED DOOR** STILL PAINTS THROUGH THE INSTALLED ADAPTER, SO IT REMAINS RATOM-FAMILY ONLY.
The rf2-k97c epic severed this coupling for the MOUNT VERBS and not for this one. Measured at
trunk, not inferred from the merges.

    tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/mount.cljs     adapter/render sites: 0   <- swap cleared these
    tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels.cljs    adapter/render sites: 2   <- :328 and :855

`render-panel!` (:328) is reached by every `mount-<panel>!` facade and by Story's
`panel-host-component`; `mount-shell!` (:855) hands `[shell/shell-view ...]` to the same door.

THE TREE ANTICIPATED THIS AND SCHEDULED IT FOR A COMMIT THAT NEVER CAME. `panels.cljs:527-531`
says in terms: *"`render-panel!` ITSELF is deliberately untouched: it is the single chokepoint where
the frame-provider and adapter/render couplings are severed for the whole embedding contract, and
that is one edit in the final commit rather than N edits now."* The epic's final child (rf2-k97c.7)
was a DOCUMENTATION bead, so no commit ever made that edit. This is a scheduling gap rather than a
rejected design.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED, AND WHAT IS NOT — read both before scoping anything.

ESTABLISHED. The shell's own mount verbs (`open!`, `open-overlay!`, `popout!`) are adapter-
indifferent: rf2-k97c.4 pinned positive rows for UIx and Fresco, and rf2-now5 added reagent-slim.
The embed door is not: it hands hiccup to `:render`, which an element-shaped substrate passes to
React untouched. Story is unaffected TODAY because Story installs stock Reagent — rf2-k97c.6's
worker verified that end to end and correctly filed nothing.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and this is the question to answer FIRST, before any code:
**is embedding Xray PANELS into an element-shaped host a use case anybody wants?** The epic's goal
was that Xray work on every browser adapter; a reasonable reading is that this is satisfied by the
shell mounting anywhere, with panel embedding a Story-shaped convenience whose only consumer
installs Reagent. **A verified "the premise does not hold — this door is deliberately ratom-family"
is a complete and good deliverable here**, and would close this bead with the reasoning recorded.

IF IT IS WANTED, the shape is already named by the comment above: ONE edit at the `render-panel!`
chokepoint, mirroring what rf2-k97c.3 did for the shell — an owned root plus a deliberate
`rf.fresco/frame-provider` seating — not N edits across the facades. Two hazards from that swap
carry over and are cheap to lose: `rf.fresco/as-component` FLATTENS a props map's keyword values
where `as-element` crosses it by identity; and a positional index into the rendered tree breaks when
the provider wrap moves.

SCOPE NOTE: `spec/API.md` and the two `api-manifest*.edn` sidecars are ONE hot-zone holding. The
Xray panel-leaf `Panel` reg-views are rostered there at the `implementation` tier, so check whether
any public name moves before assuming this is internal.
notes:
=== SITE 1 OF rf2-zaat MOVES HERE, 2026-09-12. Whoever rules this bead's question also owns a one-sentence prose correction that falls out of the ruling either way. ===

rf2-zaat carried two stale-prose sites. Site 2 (shell.cljs's self-contradicting docstring) merged as
PR #9713. **Site 1 cannot be written until THIS bead's question is answered**, so it is recorded
here verbatim rather than held on a second bead waiting for the same ruling.

THE SITE: `tools/story/deps.edn`, the `day8/re-frame2-xray` `:exclusions` rationale, under the
heading "THE STATED REPLACEMENT (this is a re-point, not a silent drop)". It reads:

    "Xray renders through re-frame.substrate.adapter and the adapter the HOST installs governs the
     runtime path, so Xray is fully served by Story's stock-Reagent adapter."

HALF-STALE SINCE rf2-k97c.3. The MOUNT VERBS (`open!`, `open-overlay!`, `popout!`) no longer render
through the host adapter at all — they paint through a `re-frame.fresco` client root Xray owns. What
IS still true is the half Story actually uses: `panels/mount-shell!` and the per-panel
`mount-<panel>!` facades still delegate to `rf.substrate.adapter/render` with a hiccup tree, so
Story's embed door really is served by its stock-Reagent adapter.

**WHICH IS THIS BEAD'S QUESTION, exactly.** If the ruling is that the embed door stays on
`adapter/render`, the sentence narrows to the embed door and stands. If the ruling is that it
follows the mount verbs onto the owned root, the sentence goes and the `:exclusions` argument needs
restating on its remaining ground. Either way it is one sentence and it is part of executing the
ruling, not a separate task.

**WHAT MUST NOT CHANGE IN EITHER DIRECTION**, and this is the clause most at risk from a careless
sweep: the `:exclusions` ITSELF and the whole argument for it. That argument is about PUBLICATION
and CLASSPATH — two jars both carrying `re_frame/adapter/reagent.cljs`, with nothing but classpath
order deciding which adapter an app gets — and the root swap does not touch any of it. The line
"THE :exclusions IS LOAD-BEARING — do not drop it (rf2-qvyr)" stands whatever is ruled here.

Both sites were verified at source at trunk 4ad6e9446a by rf2-k97c.7's worker, who routed them out
of that PR with a reason rather than deferring them for lack of time: taking them there would have
widened a markdown-only PR's gate surface, which .7's fence forbade in terms for `tools/story`.
Merged-PR audit #9713 follow-up: rf2-52rj separately tracks the outstanding tools/story/deps.edn render-coupling scope correction (rf2-zaat site 1). The shell.cljs site-2 correction is verified. This forward pointer preserves existing notes and closure fields; it is not mayor notification or acknowledgment.

=== CORRECTION 2026-09-12: SITE 1 DOES NOT WAIT ON THIS BEAD AFTER ALL. The merged-PR audit refuted my fence and it is right. ===

The note above moves rf2-zaat's site 1 here on the ground that its replacement sentence "cannot be
written until THIS bead's question is answered". **That is wrong, and the audit of PR #9713 said why
in one line:** *"No runtime migration, new API or decision about future element-shaped panel
embedding is required to describe today's split accurately."*

MY ERROR, named because the shape of it recurs: I assumed the sentence had to state the FINAL

title: docs(CLAUDE.md): catalogue item (t) — \b after a punctuation character never matches before a space, ) or newline, so a symbol-ending-in-bang census silently reads zero
description:
Add a new lettered entry — it will be **(t)** — to the instrument-misreport catalogue in
`CLAUDE.md` § Workflow, the bullet that opens "Ways the INSTRUMENTS misreport on this machine".
Items (a) through (s) exist; (t) is the next letter. **Re-derive that roster before writing** — the
bullet's own opening sentence warns that a count in it goes stale first, and it has already carried
the word FIVE while there were six.

## The defect

`\b` PLACED AFTER A PUNCTUATION CHARACTER CAN NEVER MATCH WHEN THE NEXT CHARACTER IS ALSO NON-WORD,
so a pattern like `\(skip!\b` matches NOTHING at any real call site — and the alternative silently
contributes zero to whatever census it sits in.

`\b` asserts a word/non-word boundary. After `!` (non-word) the boundary exists only if the next
character is a word character. At a real call site the next character is a space, a newline or `)`,
all non-word — so no boundary, no match.

## Measured, both directions

Against four real call-site shapes — `(skip! off-browser)`, `(skip!` then a newline,
`(skip! ":node-test: no DOM")`, and the zero-arity `(skip!)`:

    pattern              space   newline   string   zero-arity
    \(skip!\b            miss    miss      miss     miss
    \(skip!              MATCH   MATCH     MATCH    MATCH
    \(skip!\s            MATCH   MATCH     MATCH    miss
    \(skip![\s)]         MATCH   MATCH     MATCH    MATCH

And the mechanism directly: `\b` after `!` reads *no boundary* before a space, a `)` and a newline,
but **MATCHES before a word character** (`!a`). **That is what makes the pattern look plausible and
lets a casual test pass** — the one context in which it works is the one nobody writes.

## Why it is dangerous here specifically, which is the part worth writing down

**This project's symbols end in punctuation by convention** — `skip!`, `assoc!`, `conj!`,
`persistent!`, `volatile!`, `flush-views!`, `browser?`, `some?`, `fn?` — so a census over this tree
reaches for `\b` around a bang or question-mark symbol constantly. Verify that claim with a count
before asserting it in the entry.

**It fails in the DEFECT-MANUFACTURING direction.** In the instance that found it, a DOM-test census
read **399 MARKED / 183 UNMARKED** where the true reading is **579 / 3**. The 183 is a plausible
worklist naming real files, so nothing on screen says it is wrong, and an auditor who trusted it would
have filed against 180 correct rows. The gap was **exactly 180** — the identical number a previous
pass produced by omitting the `skip!` spelling altogether. **Two passes failing in the same place by
different mechanisms** is the detail that makes the entry worth its space: getting the spelling into
the pattern is not the same as getting it to match.

It was caught ONLY because the dispatch brief carried a control number to check against.

## Relationship to the entries already there — state it, do not fold them together

Same FAMILY as **(j)** (`\]` inside an ERE bracket expression silently narrowing a pattern) — a
regex that is syntactically fine and semantically near-empty, returning an honest-looking count. But a
DIFFERENT MECHANISM: (j) is a bracket class closing early, this is a zero-width assertion that cannot
hold at the position written.

Also the COMPLEMENT of **(g)**, which records that `\b` matches ACROSS A HYPHEN and so over-reports
(`host-transient` answering for `transient`). (g) is `\b` matching where you did not want it; this is
`\b` failing to match where you did. **Cross-reference both and keep all three distinct.**

## The guard

Match the SPELLING you mean and let the delimiter be explicit: `\(skip![\s)]`, or drop the assertion
entirely where the open paren already anchors the left side. Where a symbol's terminal character is
punctuation, `\b` after it is almost always wrong — and per the catalogue's standing rule, **take the
control from the target**: run the pattern once against a site it must find.

## Scope and fence

`CLAUDE.md` only, one new lettered entry, plus the minimal cross-reference edits in (g) and (j) if
you judge them warranted — say either way. **Do not renumber or restructure the existing entries** and
do not "tidy" the bullet; it is long by design.

## The CR hazard, which is this file's own documented trap and is NOT optional

Item **(e)** records that writing an entry here once inserted four real carriage returns where an
escape was meant literally, git reclassified the file from `w/crlf` to `w/-text`, stopped normalising
it, and staged **156 changed lines for a one-clause edit**.

**Measured at dispatch (re-derive at your tip): CR 156, CRLF 156, bare CR 0.** After editing, confirm
total CR still equals CRLF and bare CR is still 0 — and take both numbers with **PYTHON reading the
bytes**, `open(p,'rb').read().count(b'\r')`, never with `grep -c`, which per item **(s)** reads 0 on
this very file and would make the check pass vacuously as `0 == 0`.

Check `git diff --stat` shows a line count consistent with your edit and not the whole file.

## Gates

Nominate by PATH. `CLAUDE.md` is repo-root markdown, so it is **outside `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`'s
roots** and inside `scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci`'s — the opposite way round from the docs tree,
and the nomination this project gets wrong most often. Prove it rather than trusting me: plant a
broken link, and report which gate goes red and which stays green.

`mkdocs build --strict` does not see repo-root markdown at all (`docs_dir` is `docs`). Search
`scripts/check_*` and `scripts/check-*` and the workflow job lists for anything else grading this path
and run it. Report every captured exit, including the zeros.

Nothing validates this file's prose or structure, so check by hand that the new entry renders as a
continuation of the existing bullet rather than escaping it — that exact defect (a nested block
rendering outside its list item) reddened `scripts/check_escaped_continuations.py` on a method-docs PR
this week.

title: story: a dead ^{:key ...} on an (if ...) call form in visual_a11y_view — no fallback key, unlike rf2-wvch
description:
A GENUINELY DEAD `^{:key ...}` IN STORY -- metadata on an `(if ...)` CALL FORM inside a `for`,
with NO working key underneath it. React receives no key for these siblings and reconciles by
index.

MAYOR-VERIFIED AT SOURCE, trunk 829cca165e, nonsense control zero:

  tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/test_mode/visual_a11y_view.cljs:248-252

      (for [[i {:keys [kind] :as row}] (map-indexed vector rows)]
        ^{:key (str kind "#" i)}
        (if (= kind :visual)
          [visual-card row]
          [a11y-card row]))

The metadata rides the `if` LIST FORM and is discarded the moment it evaluates; the returned
vector carries none of it.

**AND THE FALLBACK IS ABSENT, which is what separates this from rf2-wvch.** The file has exactly
TWO real `:key` sites -- 163 and 249; every other `:key`-looking hit is `:keys` destructuring.
`a11y-card` (179-203) and `visual-card` (204-230) both return a `[:div {:style ... :data-test ...}]`
carrying NO `:key`. So nothing supplies one by another route.

=== A SECOND SITE IN THE SAME FILE THAT IS *NOT* THIS BUG ===

`visual_a11y_view.cljs:163` carries `^{:key (str rule "#" i)}` on a VECTOR LITERAL (`[:li {...}]`)
inside `findings-list`'s `for`. Reader metadata rides the vector the reader produces, and Reagent
reads metadata THEN props, so that key DOES reach React today. It is the rf2-twil class -- latent,
dying only if/when Story's view layer migrates to Fresco, whose codec reads `:key` from the
ATTRIBUTE MAP and reads Clojure metadata nowhere.

**Repair both, but do not conflate them in the commit message**: 249 is a live defect, 163 is
future-proofing. Moving each key into the returned hiccup's attribute map satisfies BOTH substrates,
because Reagent reads meta then props.

=== HOW TO TEST IT, AND THE TRAP THAT MAKES A TEST HOLLOW ===

**Do NOT assert with `(meta ...)`.** It reads `nil` at a REPAIRED site too, because the key then
lives in the attribute map -- so a metadata assertion is hollow in BOTH directions, green on broken
code and red on fixed code. Assert at the RENDERER that React actually receives the key: read
`.-key` off real React elements, as the rf2-wvch gate does
(`tools/xray/test/.../panels/epoch/view_cljs_test.cljs`, merged in #9626) -- that pattern transfers
directly. Apply the mechanical check: delete the signal, keep the fault; the row must go red.

=== PROVENANCE, AND WHY THE CENSUS SCOPE MATTERS ===

Found by the rf2-wvch worker (epochkey-a) after it noticed its FIRST census was scoped to
`tools/xray/src` and was therefore too narrow. Re-run over the full tracked roster (2956 files) it
read **333 `^{:key` hits across 128 files -- 271 vector literals, 61 prose, and exactly 1 call
form**, that one being this site. Instrument positively controlled (it flagged the pre-fix xray
site). So this is believed to be the ONLY remaining call-form instance in the tree, and the narrow
first scope is why it nearly went unseen.
notes:
WORKER REPORT (storykey-a) — PR #9634 open, not a draft.

Three commits on worker/storykey-a:
  1. fix: `visual-a11y-section`'s dead `^{:key ...}` on the `(if ...)` call
     form -> a keyed Fragment `[:<> {:key ...} (if ...)]`, the in-tree
     substrate-neutral spelling used by tools/xray static/flows/panel.cljs.
  2. refactor: `findings-list`'s LATENT `^{:key ...}` on the `[:li ...]`
     vector literal -> the `:li`'s own attribute map. Separate commit
     because it is future-proofing, not a live defect.
  3. test: tools/story/test/re_frame/story/ui/test_mode/
     visual_a11y_keys_cljs_test.cljs — asserts at the RENDERER
     (`.-key` off `r/as-element` elements), not with `(meta ...)`.

HOLLOW-GATE CHECK, three directions, all measured:
  A. `^{:key ...}` restored on the `(if ...)` call form -> section row RED,
     reads [nil nil nil]; findings row stayed GREEN.
  B. `<li>` attrs `:key` deleted -> findings row RED, reads [nil nil nil];
     section row stayed GREEN.
  C. ORIGINAL `^{:key ...}` restored on the `[:li ...]` VECTOR LITERAL ->
     GREEN, which is correct and is the evidence that site was LATENT, not
     dead. Reagent reads metadata on a vector literal, so React got the key.
     Confirms the bead's own two-severity split at the renderer.

GATES: npm run test:cljs (full node-test) GREEN — 11602 tests / 58149
assertions, 0 failures. tools/story `clojure -M:test` GREEN — 1914 tests /
7047 assertions, 0 failures, but stated honestly as NOT evidence for this
diff: it is the JVM lane and compiles neither changed file (the view is

examples_compile, tools_jvm, mcp_conformance, story_xray_browser; the rest
left to CI.

NOTHING IN THE BRIEF WAS CONTRADICTED. Both sites, both severities and the
absence of a fallback key all reproduced as described.

title: fresco: witness a hosted <ViewTransition> around Fresco children (Suspense lazy-island reveal + useDeferredValue projection); recipe in 21-code-splitting.md only if green
description:
Blocked on rf2-4ale (React 19.3 on trunk). Discovered from rf2-3y09 and from a second, independent analysis of the same release (ai/findings/react19.md, since deleted; its substance is here and on rf2-4ale).

WHAT: the witness that docs/design/fresco/product/lanes/react-compatibility-notes.md section "Experimental features stay at the host edge" already prescribes -- "prove that a hosted ViewTransition can contain Fresco children without ownership or controlled-input breakage" -- which could not run while the API was canary and can now, because `<ViewTransition>` is stable in 19.3 (https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition). Two arms:

(a) SUSPENSE REVEAL. docs/core/fresco/21-code-splitting.md:117-165 already teaches React.lazy islands under `(h/defhost suspense react/Suspense ...)`. Wrap that host in `(h/defhost view-transition react/ViewTransition {:server :render})` and witness the skeleton->content reveal animating, with a controlled input inside the Fresco children.

(b) useDeferredValue BRIDGE. A UIx island doing `(use-deferred-value (use-sub ...))` re-renders the deferred subtree in a Transition lane, so a `<ViewTransition>` around that subtree should animate. This is the ONE honest path from re-frame2 state to a View Transition: it displays an older projection briefly, defers no app-db commit, and descendants that call h/sub or n/use-sub themselves bypass it. Keep the deferred input identity-stable (React compares by identity).

THE CEILING THIS BEAD MUST NOT CONTRADICT: React's ViewTransition reference lists `useSyncExternalStore`-driven updates and updates inside `flushSync` as NOT activating it. Every ordinary re-frame2 view update is one or the other (implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:3535 useSyncExternalStore; flush-render! is react-dom/flushSync, :2067). So an ordinary dispatch animates nothing; wrapping rf/dispatch in startTransition is NOT a sound integration (the router queues, and external-store mutations cannot be non-blocking Transitions); and the lane doc's section "External-store transitions have a real ceiling" stays as written. rf2-4ale corrects only the "remains Canary/Experimental" sentence.

CHECKS: animation activation, interruption (a second update mid-animation), intent routing during the animation, unmount cleanup, prefers-reduced-motion (React does not honour it -- CSS must), hydration, and a browser without the View Transition API. And the SERVER half: react-dom/server rendering `<ViewTransition>` as a pass-through of its children is EXPECTED but must be witnessed, because `:server :render` depends on it. The raw `[:>]` escape omits its subtree on the server, so a naive `[:> react/ViewTransition ...]` around existing content DELETES that content from the response -- use a declared host with an intentional :server policy.

DELIVERABLE: the witness test(s), on the browser lane, each row asserting its own premise (the body ran; the transition fired) before the claim. A recipe in 21-code-splitting.md ONLY if green and comprehensible.

NOT THIS BEAD: a core wrapper or hiccup head (demand criterion unmet); motion/presence on View Transitions (presence exits are external-store driven -- it would animate exits and not enters, half a mechanism); addTransitionType in the routing artefact (a route change is an app-db change; if used at all it lives inside a host-local Transition around an already-resolved destination, and it is not a new dispatch option).
notes:
=== WITNESS RESULT (worker vtwitness-a, PR #9587, 2026-09-10) — MIXED, AND THEREFORE NO RECIPE ===

VERDICT. The witness landed and is green on the browser lane. The conditional deliverable is NOT
taken: docs/core/fresco/21-code-splitting.md is UNTOUCHED. The composition holds for CONTENT and
fails for INTERACTION, so a recipe would have shipped a pattern that silently discards user input.

THE BLOCKING FINDING, with its controls. A click inside a subtree the hosted <ViewTransition> is
animating LANDS ON THE DOM and produces NO app-db write — not late, not queued, not replayed once
the animation ends, and with nothing on any console channel to say so. Four readings from one row:
  * the same click on a QUIET document                              -> app-db in ~1 ms
  * a NATIVE listener on the same node, during the animation        -> fires (the click really landed)
  * a direct rf/dispatch during the SAME live animation             -> app-db in ~6 ms
  * the intent's own write, during the animation                    -> ABSENT at 3000 ms, and still
                                                                       absent after the animation settles
The mechanism is DELIBERATELY NOT ESTABLISHED. Ruled out, each by its own control on an isolated
React page: the browser (a native listener fires throughout a live transition, 4/4), React's event
delivery (onClick fires throughout, 4/4), task scheduling (setTimeout, MessageChannel, microtasks
and requestAnimationFrame all fire within a few ms of a live transition, on a small page and on a
3000-paragraph one), and the router (the direct dispatch above). That is the open question this
bead hands on; it is NOT a codec or lowering change, and no such change was made.

AN EARLIER DRAFT OF THAT ROW WAS WRONG AND IS WORTH RECORDING. It claimed the intent CANCELS the
transition, citing React's "A flushSync update cancelled a View Transition" warning. The warning is
real but it comes from the row's OWN teardown (mount/unmount! is flushSync), not from the dispatch:
the captured console.warn list is EMPTY at the moment of the claim. The claim was removed. Anyone
re-opening this should not resurrect it.

THE CEILING IS CONFIRMED, NOT CONTRADICTED, and confirmed three ways rather than one:
  * an ordinary rf/dispatch under a hosted ViewTransition -> 0 transitions started;
  * rf/dispatch inside startTransition -> 0. The router QUEUES, so the app-db write happens after
    the transition scope has already closed. That is the first of the two reasons the spelling is
    unsound;
  * dispatch-sync inside startTransition -> 0. This takes the queue out of the argument entirely —
    the store really does mutate inside the scope — and it still activates nothing, because an
    external-store mutation cannot be a non-blocking Transition. That is the second reason, and the
    one that would survive any amount of work on the router.
All three zeros are read through the SAME instrument as a plain useState update inside
startTransition under the SAME host, which DOES activate. So the zeros are the ceiling and not a
dead spy. The lane doc's "External-store transitions have a real ceiling" section is UNTOUCHED.

ARM (b), useDeferredValue BRIDGE — HOLDS. useDeferredValue over n/use-sub re-renders the deferred
subtree in a Transition lane and the surrounding <ViewTransition> animates it: startViewTransition
called, the boundary's own onUpdate fired, and named pseudo-element animations running at ready.
The bead's bypass claim is confirmed by measurement rather than asserted: at the blocking commit the
deferred subtree still paints the OLD projection ("A") while a descendant calling n/use-sub for
itself already shows the NEW one ("B"). Deferred inputs are kept identity-stable (strings).

ARM (a), SUSPENSE REVEAL — HOLDS. A react/lazy island under a declared suspense host, under the
ViewTransition host, animates skeleton->content. A controlled input among the Fresco children keeps
its subscribed value across the reveal and still round-trips through app-db afterwards. Ownership
after the reveal is exact.

THE SERVER HALF — HOLDS, AND THE TRAP REPRODUCES. A declared (h/defhost view-transition
react/ViewTransition {:server :render}) passes its Fresco children through react-dom/server; the
bare [:> react/ViewTransition ...] escape DELETES them from the response, with a premise row proving
those same children DO reach a server response when nothing wraps them. Hydration over that server
HTML reports nothing on any of React's three channels.

ALSO WITNESSED: interruption (two transition-lane updates, both settle, DOM lands on the newest);
unmount mid-animation (no window errors, zero residue); prefers-reduced-motion (React does NOT
consult it — with the CSS rule installed the transition still starts and onUpdate still fires, while
no old/new pseudo animation runs, so CSS is what stops the motion); and a browser with no View
Transition API (commits correctly, no errors, onUpdate never fires).

A MEASUREMENT WORTH CARRYING OFF THIS BEAD EVEN IF NOTHING ELSE IS: REACT'S ViewTransition
CALLBACKS ARE VIEWPORT-GATED. React reaches onUpdate only when
measureViewTransitionHostInstancesRecursive reports a host instance inside the viewport. Measured
twice in each direction on a bare React page: element at the top of the viewport ->
startViewTransition 1, onUpdate 1, five named pseudo animations; a 5000px spacer above it ->
startViewTransition still 1, onUpdate 0, two named animations — and the DOM commits correctly
either way. fresh-container! appends to document.body, which on this lane is the bottom of a
ninety-namespace cljs-test-display report, so the witness pins its container to the top of the
viewport. That is LOAD-BEARING, not cosmetic: the first run read a live mechanism as a dead one.
The application-facing consequence is the same — a region scrolled out of view gets the transition
without the callback.

DELIBERATELY LEFT STANDING:
  * docs/core/fresco/21-code-splitting.md — untouched. The condition for the recipe is not met.
  * The lane doc's ceiling section — untouched. Only the final section ("New host capabilities stay
    at the host edge"), which is where the request for this proof lives, gained three appended
    paragraphs recording the answer.
  * No core wrapper, no hiccup head, no motion/presence work, no addTransitionType — all four are
    NOT THIS BEAD per the description, and none was touched.
  * implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/codec.cljs and .../fresco/server.cljs — the
    parallel worker's surface for rf2-26hs / rf2-4sys. The witness needed no lowering change.
  * shadow-cljs.edn — hot zone, and no change was needed: the witness namespace ends
    -dom-cljs-test so the existing :browser-test ns-regexp picks it up.

LINE NUMBERS IN THE DESCRIPTION, CHECKED AT SOURCE AT THIS TIP — all three still correct:
implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:3535 is
(React/useSyncExternalStore subscribe-fn get-snap get-snap); :2067 is (react-dom/flushSync f) inside
flush-render! (the defn opens at :2055); docs/core/fresco/21-code-splitting.md:117 is the "Lazy
islands with Suspense" heading and the section runs to :180.

GATES, every exit code captured by the runner itself, unpiped, on the final rebased base:
test:browser 0 (876 tests / 4841 assertions, 0 failures — the count moving 862 -> 876 across the
rebase is itself the proof the re-run was on the new base); test:cljs 0 (11525 / 57901, 0 failures);

are, and both are green.

SABOTAGE CONTROL. useDeferredValue removed from the bridge island, one anchor, match count read as
1 BEFORE the run. The lane came back exit 1 with 5 failures, ALL FIVE in the bridge row, naming
exactly what was removed: started 0, onUpdate 0, no animations, no named animations, and the bypass
split reading {:deferred "B" :self "B"} instead of {:deferred "A" :self "B"}. Every other row stayed
green — the fault existed only in this tree, which is the discrimination. Restored and verified by
git BLOB hash 8354d5b681172ec095747f5fc6206834335e8b68, identical before the plant and after the
restore and equal to the committed object. Edits were committed before the plant.

INSTRUMENT NOTES FOR THE CATALOGUE (measured this session, on this box):
  * rf2-4ale's close_reason was ERASED by the audit reopen, exactly as CLAUDE.md predicts, so the
    brief's instruction to read it was unsatisfiable at tip. Recovered from bd history rf2-4ale
    --json (5th snapshot from newest, 7327 chars) and used from there.

title: ci(classifier): tools/template/* does not arm the surface that schedules jvm-uix, so a template change cannot red the uix recipe test (one-directional coupling; rf2-v37n post-mortem)
description:
Filed from the rf2-v37n post-mortem. The uixdom-a worker swept the classifier and gave this a
sharp shape, so the analysis below is its finding rather than a hypothesis to re-derive — but
re-verify at source before changing anything.

## What happened

PR #9543 deliberately dropped `com.pitch/uix.dom` from the UIx template (ruled: the Root is minted
by the shared spine via `react-dom/client`). `uix_consumer_deps_recipe_test.clj` still asserted the
template pinned BOTH coordinates. That check read **SKIPPED** on #9543 because its diff armed
`template_expensive` and nothing else. It surfaced only on PR #9550, whose diff armed the
uix-adapter surface for unrelated reasons — by which point trunk had been red for a while and an
unrelated PR was wearing the failure.

Fixed under rf2-v37n in PR #9553. **This bead is about the scheduling gap, not the test.**

## The gap, precisely — it is ONE-DIRECTIONAL

- `implementation/adapters/*` **does** arm `template_expensive`. An adapter change therefore
  schedules the template suite.
- `tools/template/*` does **not** arm `adapter_diagnostic`, which is the surface that schedules
  `jvm-uix`.

So the coupling exists in one direction only, and **the missing edge is exactly the one that would
have caught this**. It is also the narrower of the two conceivable additions, which is the argument
for doing it rather than reaching for something broader.

## Why the merge criterion cannot catch this class

Clause 2 accepts passed-OR-SKIPPED. That is correct and must stay — a skipped check on an
unaffected surface is the classifier working. So a diagnostic the classifier never scheduled is
admitted structurally, by design, and no amount of care at merge time sees it. **The repair belongs
in the classifier, not in the merge rule.** Do NOT propose a sixth merge clause.

## Scope

Decide whether `tools/template/*` should arm the surface that schedules `jvm-uix`, and if so add
that one edge. `.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh` and its mirror
`implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs` are ONE HOLDING and hot-zone one-toucher: the
test pins the script's outputs, so a change to what the classifier emits lands a tree where the
suite contradicts the script unless both halves move in ONE commit.

Weigh the cost honestly before adding it: arming a heavier surface from a frequently-touched
directory buys coverage with CI minutes on every template PR. If the conclusion is that the edge is
not worth its cost, that is a legitimate outcome — record the reasoning and close. Do not widen
beyond this one edge, and do not add a new gate.

visibly distinct from the second, which is what makes the second a finding.

title: spec/005: re-validate and re-pin the XState citations against a named 6.0.0-alpha — the parallel-broadcast one now cites behaviour v6 corrected, and re-frame2 already has the newer semantics
description:
From the 2026-09-07 XState v6 parity review (rf2-2qfi).

=== THE PROBLEM, AND IT IS A DOCUMENTATION HAZARD RATHER THAN A BUG ===
spec/005-StateMachines.md anchors several of its most load-bearing semantic decisions to XState v5, by name and sometimes by exact version. Mike ruled on 2026-06-22 to fully target v6, and EP-0029 retargeted the API SHAPE — but these interpretation-level citations were not revisited, because EP-0029 barely touches the interpretation algorithm at all (it has no section on microsteps, macrosteps, transition selection, conflict resolution or document order; the two incidental mentions of "transition selection" are both inside the :internal-events section).

The behaviour is, as far as this review could establish, FINE. In one case it is better than the citation suggests. The hazard is that the citations now point at semantics XState itself has moved away from, and a future reader doing exactly what this review did — checking re-frame2 against current XState — could "correct" re-frame2 toward the superseded behaviour on the spec's own authority.

=== THE SPECIFIC CITATIONS ===

1. THE DANGEROUS ONE. spec/005 line 1703, on parallel transition broadcast: "The broadcast is select-then-apply (two-phase — XState v5 / SCXML parity, verified against xstate@5.32.0)". Two-phase select-then-apply is not the issue and is SCXML-correct. The issue is the neighbouring behaviour that citation implicitly blesses. XState v6 alpha.17 changed parallel transition domains in two ways: "A transition targeting a state inside one region no longer exits and resets sibling regions", and "A cross-region transition (source in one region, target in another) now only exits the region containing its targets. The source region and other sibling regions stay in their current states." re-frame2 ALREADY behaves the v6 way — line 1715: "Regions that didn't transition keep their prior value in place." So re-frame2 anticipated a correction XState shipped later, while citing as its authority the version that had the old behaviour. ACTION: re-pin this to v6 and state plainly that sibling regions are never reset, so the property reads as intentional rather than incidental.

2. THE IMPRECISE ONE. spec/005 §Transition resolution: "This is XState v5's transition-selection order". The specific rule re-frame2 implements — exact descriptor tried first, and if all its guards fail the matching wildcard descriptors are tried as a fallback rather than being skipped — did not arrive in XState at v5.0. It landed at 5.32.2: "When a state has both an exact event descriptor and a matching wildcard descriptor, transitions from the exact descriptor are now tried first; if all their guards fail, matching wildcard descriptor transitions are tried as fallback." re-frame2 matches current behaviour exactly, including the guard-fallback subtlety and the worked :mouse/down example. ACTION: cite the version the rule actually appeared in. A reader checking against an early v5 would find a genuine mismatch and think re-frame2 wrong.

3. THE ONE AT RISK OF CONFLATION. spec/005 §Transition resolution: "xstate-v5 parity (do not 'fix' this back to an error): xstate v5 removed the v4 strict flag — an event with no transition in the current state is simply ignored". Still true in v6 for UNHANDLED events. But v6 alpha.50 introduced rejection at the delivery boundary for INVALID events, and the two are easy to conflate when skim-reading a v6 changelog. ACTION: add one sentence distinguishing them, so the next reviewer does not read alpha.50 as overturning the no-op rule. rf2-1r69 is the bead that actually acts on alpha.50.

=== WHAT THIS BEAD IS NOT ===
NOT a behaviour change. If re-validation turns up a place where re-frame2's behaviour genuinely differs from 6.0.0-alpha.52 and the difference is not already a recorded decision, that is a NEW bead with its own argument — do not fold a behaviour change into a citation refresh, and do not change behaviour to chase an alpha.

=== BOUND THE WORK: PIN A VERSION AND SAY SO ===
v6 is at 6.0.0-alpha.52 with no stable release (latest is 5.32.6). EP-0029 C17 already rejected alpha-churn exactness, and that stands. So the deliverable is NOT "track v6" — it is: re-validate these citations once against a NAMED alpha, write that alpha's version into the spec text so the next reader knows exactly what was checked and when, and stop. A citation that says which version it was verified against is self-dating and ages honestly; one that says "v5" does not.

The existing "verified against xstate@5.32.0" phrasing is the right pattern and should be kept, just updated — whoever wrote it had this exact problem in mind.

GATES: spec/005-StateMachines.md is a hot-zone file, so this sequences against other machine-spec work. Docs-only change; mkdocs build --strict covers spec/ via the staging hook, and check_doc_slugs.py validates the anchors.
acceptance_criteria: Citations re-pinned to a named alpha version; the sibling-region non-reset property stated as intentional; the exact-before-wildcard rule cited to the version it appeared in; unhandled-versus-invalid distinguished in one sentence. No behaviour change.
notes: Merged-PR audit #9388 (da745431e407e95d0459fa8d8c2edc18d235b08a): the version pins, wildcard fallback version and invalid/unhandled distinction are delivered. Reopen this documentation owner for the newly added spec/005-StateMachines.md:1717 cross-region claim. The paragraph now says a transition sourced in one region can target another while preserving the source, and claims re-frame2 anticipated this XState fix. That goes beyond the existing non-reset guarantee. parallel.cljc:233-277 builds an isolated synthetic machine from each region; :915-937 selects/applies its transitions inside that region. Only the root fallback normalizes region-qualified targets (:1050-1154). Actual landed public machines/machine-transition probe: root :on {:go {:target [:b :two]}} on {a:one,b:one} yields {a:one,b:two}; placing that target under region a state's :on yields {a:[:b :two],b:one}, not the claimed cross-region result (exit 0, exact archived core/flows/schemas/machines sources, ai/pr-audit-9388/gate-cross-region-re-frame2-1.log). This invalid/unsupported regional spelling is evidence that the prose must not advertise it, not a request to broaden the runtime. Scope the new paragraph to the supported local/root-target non-reset behavior and identify cross-region targeting as the cited upstream behavior unless separately established. Preserve the original no-behavior-change fence; any proposed parity capability needs its own argument as the original brief requires. Upstream primary changelog confirms the cited alpha.17 change, but that citation alone does not establish re-frame2 parity: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/statelyai/xstate/refs/heads/next/packages/core/CHANGELOG.md .
close_reason: PR #9399. #9388 had already delivered the version pins, the 5.32.2 wildcard-fallback citation and the unhandled-versus-invalid distinction; this closes the audit's reopen. The cross-region claim added at spec/005:1717 was verified WRONG at source (build-region-machine in implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/parallel.cljc builds a synthetic single-machine spec from the region body alone, so a region-local target resolves inside that region; only apply-root-region-target normalises region-qualified targets). The paragraph now claims only the non-reset guarantee re-frame2 has, and a scope note identifies cross-region targeting as cited upstream behaviour. No behaviour change. The runtime question is rf2-ovhj. Version facts re-taken from primary sources 2026-09-07: registry dist-tags latest=5.32.6 beta=5.0.0-beta.54 alpha=6.0.0-alpha.52, and the xstate next-branch packages/core/CHANGELOG.md.

title: spec: align 005/011 + docs to the shipped SSR :after hydration rule — RULED full client-resolved delay from the client arm, epoch retained, no entry replay; zero code change (the bead's XState v6 premise is refuted in notes)
description:
From the 2026-09-07 XState v6 parity review (rf2-2qfi). NEEDS A RULING, not implementation — the question is which of two defensible semantics re-frame2 wants, and only Mike can settle it.

=== WHAT re-frame2 DOES TODAY ===
An in-flight :after timer is CANCELLED on restore. spec/005-StateMachines.md line 2506 lists :on-restore as one of the six closed cancellation reasons on :rf.machine.timer/cancelled, glossed: "epoch restore unwound the bearing epoch — the in-flight host-clock handle is released eagerly so the orphaned timer never fires against the restored state."

re-frame2 persists no wall-clock start for a timer. :rf/after-epoch (and :rf/after-epoch-by-region for parallel machines) is a per-scheduling-node COUNTER, and staleness is decided facts-against-facts by comparing the carried epoch to the node's current entry, never by comparing wall-clocks. Spec line 2483 makes that deliberate: comparing wall-clocks would put a host read into a durable decision and break replay determinism.

=== WHAT v6 DID ===
alpha.41 (durable): "Timers persisted from a running actor carry their wall-clock start (startedAt); restoring the snapshot schedules the remaining time toward the original deadline (clamped to the declared delay), so a timer past due fires immediately instead of restarting its full delay."

Three distinct commitments: persist a wall-clock origin; on restore schedule the REMAINDER rather than the full delay; clamp so a corrupt or future-dated origin cannot extend the timer beyond what was declared.

=== WHY re-frame2's CHOICE IS RIGHT FOR THE CASE IT WAS DESIGNED FOR ===
re-frame2's restore contract serves TIME-TRAVEL DEBUGGING (Tool-Pair epoch restore) and SSR HYDRATION. For time travel, cancelling is plainly correct — rewinding to an earlier snapshot must not resume a wall-clock deadline that belongs to a future that has been rewound away, and firing a past-due timer immediately on a rewind would be a debugger that mutates the state you rewound to look at. v6's rule would be actively wrong there. This bead is NOT proposing to adopt v6 wholesale.

=== WHERE THE GAP ACTUALLY BITES, AND IT IS NARROW ===
Two places, and only two:

1. SSR HYDRATION HANDOFF — ALREADY UNSPECIFIED, BY ADMISSION. :after no-ops entirely under SSR (spec line 2475), so the server schedules nothing; the client must start the timers after hydration. Spec line 2477 then says, verbatim: "The first client render after hydration can re-fire entry actions to begin scheduling, depending on the implementation's hydration policy — the spec leaves the hydration-handoff timing to the host so long as the snapshot value is preserved." That is a deliberate hole, and v6 has now published a considered answer to the structurally identical question. Worth deciding rather than leaving to each host, because two hosts making opposite choices is an interop difference nobody will notice until a timer fires twice or never.

2. DURABLE / RESUMED WORKFLOWS — a machine persisted and resumed hours later, where "restart the full 30-minute deadline" and "the deadline passed while you were away" are genuinely different products. This is downstream of EP-0029 B2 (Durable workflow steps), classified "For Later Consideration - but Probably not". If B2 stays rejected this half of the bead is moot and should be closed as such; it is recorded so the connection is visible when B2 is next revisited, NOT to reopen B2.

=== THE RULING WANTED ===
Whether the clamped-remaining-time rule should govern the SSR hydration handoff specifically — leaving time-travel restore cancelling exactly as it does now. Three options:
  (a) Specify clamped-remaining for hydration, borrowing v6's rule including the clamp and the fire-immediately-if-past-due behaviour. Closes a spec hole; costs a persisted wall-clock origin in the hydration payload only, not in the durable snapshot.
  (b) Specify full-restart-on-hydration. Also closes the hole, keeps every wall-clock read out of the snapshot, and matches the existing "restart from the current moment" reasoning already written at spec line 2378 for the adjacent dynamic-delay case — which argues restart semantics is the simplest mental model and that extending or shortening makes the wall-clock interaction non-monotonic. That argument transfers.
  (c) Leave it host-defined. Status quo; the hole stays.
RECOMMENDATION: (b). It closes the hole, it is consistent with reasoning re-frame2 has ALREADY written down and defended for the neighbouring case, and it keeps the replay-determinism posture of spec line 2483 intact without a special case. v6's rule is the better answer for durable workflows and the worse answer for a framework whose restore path is dominated by debugging and hydration.

If (a) or (b) is chosen, the change is a spec/005 edit plus the SSR spec (011) — spec/005 is a hot-zone file, so sequence it. If (c), close this bead saying so; leaving it open as a permanent open question is worse than a recorded decision.
acceptance_criteria: A recorded ruling: clamped-remaining, full-restart, or explicitly host-defined. If not host-defined, spec/005 and spec/011 updated to say which.
notes:
--- MAYOR 2026-09-08 15:5x AUSEST — PREMISES RE-VERIFIED AT SOURCE; CITATIONS DRIFTED, FACTS HELD ---
I applied the "which of these actually need Mike" test to this bead and it PASSES — unlike rf2-hu69,
which I took off the list this tick, this one has no measurement half left to dispatch. Its own text says
"NEEDS A RULING, not implementation", and its "what re-frame2 does today" section is already answered
with spec citations. So the only useful thing a coordinator can do is make sure those citations still
resolve before Mike rules on them. I did that, on origin/main at 2f9fdc15d9.
ALL THREE FACTUAL CLAIMS HOLD. The LINE NUMBERS HAVE DRIFTED BY ABOUT THIRTEEN — spec/005 has been edited
several times since this bead was filed on 2026-09-07 — so cite the construct, not the line:
  * ":on-restore is one of the six closed cancellation reasons on :rf.machine.timer/cancelled" — bead
    cites :2506, now at :2519. The gloss is verbatim as the bead quotes it: "epoch restore unwound the
    bearing epoch — the in-flight host-clock handle is released eagerly so the orphaned timer never fires
    against the restored state". The six reasons are intact: :on-exit, :on-destroy, :on-resolution,
    :on-supersede, :on-frame-destroy, :on-restore.
  * "comparing wall-clocks would put a host read into a durable decision and break replay determinism" —
    bead cites :2483, now at :2496, and the tree states it MORE strongly than the bead does. That
    paragraph is headed "Timer scheduling is the one ambient-clock exception": reading the host clock to
    SCHEDULE a fire-and-forget timer is sanctioned, and the decision the timer drives is gated
    facts-against-facts by the per-scheduling-node epoch, "never by comparing wall-clocks".
  * ":rf/after-epoch is a per-scheduling-node COUNTER, with :rf/after-epoch-by-region for parallel
    machines" — holds; the reserved-snapshot-key table at :80 spells out the per-node keying and why a
    single scalar could not keep a parent's timer live across a child transition.
WHY THAT LAST POINT MATTERS TO THE RULING RATHER THAN BEING TRIVIA: v6's alpha.41 rule requires
persisting a WALL-CLOCK ORIGIN. This tree deliberately persists no wall-clock start at all, and the
paragraph above is the written reason. So "adopt v6's clamped-remaining" is not a small semantic tweak —
it introduces the first durable wall-clock into the machine snapshot, against a rule the spec argues for
at length. The bead's own recommendation (full-restart, not v6's rule) is consistent with that, and this
check strengthens it rather than changing it.
SEQUENCING NOTE FOR WHOEVER ACTS ON THE RULING: spec/005-StateMachines.md is currently held by
worker/hu69-a (rf2-hu69, the :final?-region measurement). Whichever way this is ruled, the spec/005 and
spec/011 edits sequence behind that PR.
--- DECISION 2026-09-08 — RULED (b), AND IT IS RATIFY-WHAT-SHIPS. NO CODE CHANGE. ---

RULING: on SSR hydration the client arms each active `:after` declaration for its FULL
CLIENT-RESOLVED delay, measured from the client arm; the hydrated snapshot's epoch is
RETAINED (never bumped) and NO entry cascade is replayed. Remaining-time / clamped /
fire-if-past-due (XState's durable-actor rule) is REJECTED for the hydration handoff.
This is exactly what the reference implementation has done since 2026-09-01, so the
deliverable is SPEC + DOCS ALIGNMENT ONLY — zero implementation, zero behaviour change.
Two independent reviews (original dossier + Codex) both landed on (b).

=== WHY (the arguments that actually carry it, after both reviews) ===
1. PRIMARY, and sufficient on its own: SSR never arms a timer server-side (spec/005:2488,
   spec/011:1590), so there is NO RUNNING COUNTDOWN TO RESUME. Nothing durable records a
   schedule instant. The client's arrival IS the entry, for timing purposes.
2. PRODUCT: under SSR `T0` means "when these bytes were produced", not "when THIS USER
   entered the state". A cached / prerendered / back-forward-cached response would make
   every `:after` past-due under a remaining-time rule — instant escalation for every
   visitor for the whole cache TTL. Write this as design rationale; Codex is right that
   repo-wide caching is a hypothetical here, not a measured deployment property.
3. SUPPORTING: Xray computes an after-ring deadline as scheduled-time + reported delay
   (tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/machine_after_rings_helpers.cljc:226), so a
   shortened arm would make the `/scheduled` row's `:delay` tag lie. Real, but it does NOT
   by itself mandate a new trace tag (Codex's correction to the dossier's cost estimate).

=== WHERE THE TWO REVIEWS CONFLICT — CODEX WINS ON ALL FOUR, AND TWO CHANGE THE DELIVERABLE ===
C1. "This diverges from XState v6" — WRONG, and the dossier's proposed spec paragraph
    announcing a deliberate divergence MUST NOT BE WRITTEN. Codex fetched the changelog
    pinned at commit 2c4eeb4881c7fab607ef2dd410e547c17f1bff87 (`git ls-remote` resolves
    BOTH `next` and `xstate@6.0.0-alpha.52` there) and the alpha.41 entry ends: "Pure-
    transition snapshots carry no timestamp and restart the declared delay." v6's clamped-
    remaining rule governs timers persisted from a RUNNING actor. re-frame2's never-armed
    SSR timer is the TIMESTAMP-FREE case, which v6 answers the SAME WAY WE DO. The original
    took the v6 quote on trust (its own §7 says so); Codex went to the primary source.
    Primary source wins. THIS ALSO REFUTES THE BEAD'S FRAMING: the bead's title and body
    assert "XState v6 alpha.41 specified the analogous case (clamped remaining time)" — the
    analogous case is the pure-transition one, and v6 restarts it.
C2. "The payload carries no clock of any kind" — FACTUALLY WRONG. `:rf/ssr-rendered-at`
    (optional, ms-since-epoch, server render completion) is ALREADY in the payload scope
    table at spec/011-SSR.md:71 and in the `HydrationPayload` schema at
    spec/Spec-Schemas.md:3918. I read both. The shared builder does not populate it
    (implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/payload_policy.cljc:776). Further, spec/005:2496
    forbids UNRECORDED AMBIENT time in durable decisions while expressly permitting declared
    recordable coeffects (`:rf/time-ms`) — it is not an absolute bar on a persisted
    timestamp. CONSEQUENCE: the dossier's headline argument — that (a) is structurally
    impossible without either a durable wall-clock in the time-travel snapshot or a second
    snapshot-parallel wire channel — is OVERSTATED and must not be recorded as the reason.
    (a) is representable. We decline it because there is no running server countdown and no
    established product requirement, NOT because time cannot be expressed. The RULING is
    unchanged; its justification moves onto points 1-2 above.
C3. "XState has no render-equivalence contract, so (a)'s collision with spec/011:52 is
    invisible to v6" — WRONG: XState's own React SSR docs require matching the first client
    render. And the CLJS timer is `setTimeout` (implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.cljs:146),
    so even a zero remainder would not synchronously mutate the snapshot. The hydration-race
    argument is UNMEASURED and is DROPPED entirely — do not put it in the spec rationale.
C4. MECHANISM: the dossier wanted to KEEP spec/011:1596's permission to "re-fire entry
    actions on hydration" as a host choice. Codex wins — that permission now CONTRADICTS the
    ruled contract, because re-firing entry replays `:entry`/`:action`/`:raise`/`:spawn` and
    bumps the epoch, whereas the ruled behaviour retains the epoch and replays nothing.
    Leaving it in leaves the spec self-contradictory, which is the very defect this bead
    exists to close. REMOVE the entry-replay permission; keep the host's private mechanics
    (which seam does the arming) unspecified.

=== LOAD-BEARING EVIDENCE — WHAT ALREADY SHIPS (read in this tree, HEAD 43a7f1b3ef) ===
implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/hydrate.cljc:60-64 — "It runs NO cascade. No
  `:entry`, no `:exit`, no `:action`, no `:raise`, no `:spawn`, no `:always` ... and no
  snapshot is written (the epoch is read, never bumped)."
implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/hydrate.cljc:66-80 — docstring section headed
  "Remaining duration: the FULL declared delay", reasoning from spec/005 §Clock abstraction:
  no `scheduled-at` / `due-at` exists on the wire, so there is no remainder to compute.
implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/hydrate.cljc:231-334 — `rearm-after-timers!`
  (reconcile at :313: cancel table entries the replacement snapshot no longer declares, then
  arm each live declaration).
implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/timer.cljc:1008-1048 — `rearm-hydrated-after-timer!`;
  ordinary scheduler at :1044; server-side scheduling skipped before delay resolution at :675;
  delay resolution at :119 (fns resolve against the hydrated snapshot, subscription delays
  against the CLIENT subscription — hence "client-resolved", not "declared literal").
implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc:269 — `reg-fx :rf.machine/hydrate-rearm`;
  :459 — the `:machines/rearm-after-hydration!` late-bind hook.
implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/hydrate.cljc:383 — the fx runs AFTER installation;
  :396-403 — conjes `[:rf.machine/hydrate-rearm {}]` onto `:rf/hydrate`'s `:fx`, gated on
  the machines artefact being loaded.

PINNED BY TWO TESTS, NOT ONE (the dossier knew only the first):
  implementation/machines/test/re_frame/machine_after_hydration_rearm_cljs_test.cljc:203-207
    — `(is (= [5000] @arms))` "armed for the FULL declared delay measured from hydration";
    epoch-not-bumped asserted at :196-199.
  implementation/ssr/test/re_frame/ssr/machine_after_rearm_cljs_test.cljc:~98-165 — the REAL
    integration path: server frame -> `build-payload` -> `dispatch-sync [:rf/hydrate payload]`.
    Asserts exactly ONE timer armed, `[5000]`, epoch == the payload's epoch, `:waiting`
    before the fire, `:timeout` after, and `:data :entries` == 1 ("`:entry` still ran exactly
    once — the server's. The re-arm reconstructs host work; it does not replay history.").
    THIS ALREADY DELIVERS the "no transition before the interval, transition at expiry"
    assertion Codex asked for — no new test is needed for the duration.

USER DOCS: docs/machines/automatic-transitions.md:237 asserts re-arming happens but says
nothing about the duration.

PROVENANCE CORRECTION (Codex, confirmed by `git log --follow` on hydrate.cljc): the behaviour
was INTRODUCED by 2de167f2ed "fix(machines): re-arm active :after timers on SSR hydration
(rf2-jqvgp)" on 2026-09-01, then repaired four times — 4c1e29b80f (reconcile, not just add),
cc91101299 (bind to one frame incarnation), 83f1bb6818 (fence the arm's own /scheduled
fan-out), 5c434220c4 (alias refactor). PR #8978 was the LAST repair, not the introduction.
The pre-rf2-jqvgp behaviour was arming NOTHING — a machine hydrated into an `:after` state
was terminal, which is the P1 that bug fixed.

CONTRADICTS THE BEAD'S OWN PREMISE — say so when editing: (i) the bead says the handoff is
undecided/host-defined; that is true of the SPEC TEXT and FALSE of the implementation, which
settled it a week before the bead was filed; (ii) the v6 analogy is backwards (C1);
(iii) "re-frame2 persists no wall-clock" is true of the SNAPSHOT but not of the PAYLOAD (C2).

CONFORMANCE GAP — REAL, AND INDEPENDENT OF THE RULING: `grep -rn 'rearm|re-arm'
spec/conformance/` returns ZERO. Control on the same tree with the same tool: `after-schedule`
hits spec/conformance/fixtures/{after-hierarchy,after-single-delay,after-stale-detection,
cross-spec-machines-under-ssr,machine-timeout-spawn-fire,machine-timeout-state-fire}.edn, so
the instrument discriminates. cross-spec-machines-under-ssr.edn:34 pins ONLY the server-side
skip. A second host implementing 005+011 from the spec alone has nothing to conform to on the
client half. Separate bead filed (below). Second negative finding from the dossier, with its
control: `hydrate-rearm` appears in 0 `.md` files repo-wide (control `after-schedule` -> 8
occurrences in 4 files).

=== THE WORK — FOUR SPEC/DOC SENTENCES, ONE PR, ONE WORKER ===
Both spec files are HOT-ZONE: 005 + 011 + the docs sentence go in ONE sequential PR.
1. spec/011-SSR.md:1596 (bullet 3 of "`:after` is no-op under SSR") — REPLACE. Currently
   permits either re-firing entry actions or a special-cased scheduler and calls the handoff
   "a host-implementation choice". New substance: on successful hydration the client installs
   the snapshot, then reconciles each ACTIVE `:after` declaration to exactly ONE timer armed
   for its FULL CLIENT-RESOLVED delay, measured from the client arm (not from server render,
   and not from "when the page becomes interactive" — name the client arm precisely). The
   hydrated epoch is RETAINED, never bumped. NO `:entry`, `:action`, `:raise`, `:spawn` or
   `:always` is replayed and no snapshot is written. Which host seam performs the arm stays
   unspecified; the DURATION, the EPOCH and the NO-REPLAY are normative.
2. spec/011-SSR.md:1603 — "the client's epoch would be DIFFERENT" contradicts the retained
   epoch. Reword so the leak argument survives without that claim.
3. spec/005-StateMachines.md:2490 — REPLACE the delegating sentence ("the spec leaves the
   hydration-handoff timing to the host so long as the snapshot value is preserved") with a
   pointer to the 011 rule plus the one-line reason: nothing durable records a schedule
   instant, so there is no remainder to compute and none is invented.
4. spec/005-StateMachines.md:2492 — the tail clause says child-actor handlers "re-establish
   on the client side via the post-hydration entry replay". There IS no entry replay.
   Reconcile.
5. docs/machines/automatic-transitions.md:237 — add the duration sentence to the existing
   "The client re-arms timers after hydration."
NO paragraph claiming divergence from XState (C1). NO render-race rationale (C3). NO claim
that a remaining-time rule is structurally impossible (C2) — the honest reason is "there is
no running server countdown to resume".

title: tools/story: three near-identical pending-atom + drain! exception collectors in frames.cljc — extract one factory
description:
SURFACE: tools/story (64,709 production lines, 5.6 mutations/kloc — the highest of the large surfaces). Found by the 2026-09-07 FP audit (rf2-5941).

THE DEFECT IS DUPLICATION, NOT MUTATION. The local atom here is CORRECT and must stay: these collectors capture exceptions arriving asynchronously from re-frame event-handler callbacks and drain them into a frame's [:rf.story/assertions] slot before the next teardown dispatch. That is a side-channel across time — there is no way to thread it functionally through dispatch, and the code says so. What is wrong is that the same closure is written out THREE TIMES.

THE THREE SITES, in tools/story/src/re_frame/story/frames.cljc:
  line 249  (frame-id, phase :phase-0-setup)             — setup decorators
  line 360  (variant-id, variant teardown)               — frame-setup-decorators teardown
  line 468  (variant-id, phase :phase-loaders-teardown)  — loaders teardown

All three are structurally identical:
  (let [pending (atom [])
        drain!  (fn [] (when-let [evs (seq @pending)]
                         (reset! pending [])
                         (doseq [tev evs]
                           (let [orig-event (get-in tev [:tags :event])
                                 err        (get-in tev [:tags :exception])
                                 record     (phase-exception-record <ID> <PHASE> orig-event err (pipeline-event-opts tev))]
                             (try (rf/dispatch-sync [::append-teardown-assertion record]) ...)))))]
    ...)

They differ ONLY in the id passed (frame-id vs variant-id) and the phase keyword. The bodies — the get-in pairs, the record construction, the reset-then-doseq drain order, the try/catch around dispatch-sync — are the same text.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. The drain order is load-bearing and subtle: 'reset! pending []' happens BEFORE the doseq so that a re-entrant capture during dispatch is not lost or double-drained, and the site at line 360 carries a nine-line comment explaining that earlier failures must be projected before a later teardown event reads the assertions slot. That reasoning is written at ONE of the three sites. A change to the ordering contract has to be made three times and the rationale is only findable at one of them — which is how the ordering silently drifts.

ACTION: extract one factory, e.g.
  (defn- exception-collector
    "Returns {:pending ... :drain! ...} ..."
    [id phase])
returning the atom and the drain! closure, and call it three times with [frame-id :phase-0-setup], [variant-id <the teardown phase>], [variant-id :phase-loaders-teardown]. Move the ordering rationale onto the factory's docstring, where it governs all three call sites. Keep the atom.

VERIFY the three phase keywords at source before extracting — this bead names two of them from the audit's reading and the middle one was not read in full; do not assume the third is symmetric.

GATES: tools/story has its own suite (clojure -M:test from tools/story/, plus npm run test:cljs for the substrate contract tests). This is a refactor with no behaviour change, so the existing story tests are the gate; do not add new ones unless extraction reveals a real asymmetry between the three sites, which is itself worth reporting.

HOT-ZONE NOTE: none of the three is a hot path — they run at frame setup/teardown, not per render or per event — so there is no perf argument for keeping three copies inlined.
acceptance_criteria: One factory; three call sites; ordering rationale on the factory docstring; story suite green; no behaviour change.
notes:
DELIVERED 2026-09-07. PR #9360, merged as 9ae1b0029c.

WHAT LANDED. One private `exception-collector` factory in
tools/story/src/re_frame/story/frames.cljc, taking [id phase] and returning
{:listener _ :drain! _}. Three call sites, as the bead asked.

THE COUNT WAS NINE, NOT THREE. The bead named the three `drain!` closures at
249/360/468. Each of those three functions ALSO carried an inlined "final drain"
block after its listener unbinds — the same body a fourth, fifth and sixth time —
and a `listener` closure identical modulo the frame id, a seventh, eighth and
ninth. The factory replaces all nine. This is why the diff is -131/+107 rather
than the smaller change the bead's three-site framing implies.

PHASE KEYWORDS, VERIFIED AT SOURCE as the bead required (it flagged that the
middle one had not been read in full and told me not to assume symmetry):
  apply-frame-setup!       frame-id    :phase-0-setup
  apply-frame-teardown!    variant-id  :phase-teardown
  apply-loaders-teardown!  variant-id  :phase-loaders-teardown
All three as the bead guessed; the middle one is confirmed rather than assumed.

THE ASYMMETRY THE BEAD PREDICTED IS REAL, AND IT IS A BUG, NOT A STYLE POINT.
apply-loaders-teardown!'s FINAL drain called phase-exception-record WITHOUT
(pipeline-event-opts tev). The other five copies of that body all passed it —
including the in-walk drain! of that same function, four lines above. So a
pipeline exception delivered after that one walk's listener unbound lost its
:operation / :failing-id attribution, where the identical event in the other two
phases kept it. Five sites agreed and one did not, which reads as a copy-paste
omission rather than an intended difference. Unifying the six repairs it.

That is THE ONLY BEHAVIOUR CHANGE in the PR, and it is the concrete instance of
the harm the bead's rationale predicted: "a change to the ordering contract has
to be made three times and the rationale is only findable at one of them — which
is how the ordering silently drifts". It had already drifted. No test pinned the
divergent shape, so nothing was red before or after.

Per the bead's gate instruction ("do not add new tests unless extraction reveals
a real asymmetry between the three sites, which is itself worth reporting") this
is reported rather than test-pinned; the belt-and-braces final-drain path is
documented in situ as one dispatch-sync should never reach.

THE ATOM STAYS, as the bead required. Exceptions arrive off the trace stream
(re-frame's interceptor chain catches handler throws and emits
:rf.error/handler-exception rather than re-throwing), so they are a side-channel
between dispatches with nothing in dispatch-sync's return to carry them. The
queue is function-local and drained empty before the walk returns.

ORDERING RATIONALE MOVED, as the acceptance criteria required. The nine-line
comment that lived at ONE of the three sites is now on the factory docstring,
stated as two numbered properties: (i) the queue is emptied BEFORE projecting so
a re-entrant capture is neither lost nor double-drained, and (ii) projection
precedes the next phase event so an event reading the assertions slot sees
earlier failures already landed.

PROPORTIONALITY. One `defn-` in the same namespace. No protocol, no new
namespace, no macro, no collector framework. No public name moves, so
spec/API.md and the api-manifest sidecars are untouched.

GATES (exit codes captured on the same command line as the redirect, never read
through a pipe):
  sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh          exit 0   PASS fast PR spine
  sh scripts/test-jvm-tools.sh        exit 0   PASS tools JVM artefacts, 10 artefacts
  clojure -M:test in tools/story      exit 0
  python scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py  exit 0

ASSERTION COUNTS, tools/story, before and after the extraction — taken by
reverting the file to its merge-base content, running, restoring, re-running,
with the restore verified by git blob hash rather than by reading a diff:
  BEFORE  1903 tests / 7010 assertions / 0 failures / 0 errors
  AFTER   1903 tests / 7010 assertions / 0 failures / 0 errors
Identical, which is the point: a refactor that silently drops a namespace from a
run also reads as green. The independent tools/story run inside
test-jvm-tools.sh reported the same 1903/7010.

SABOTAGE CONTROL. `tools/story` is in NO tier of the fast-PR spine (the script's
own header says so), so the spine alone would have returned a green that
inspected nothing here. Beyond running the suite directly: swapping the
:phase-teardown argument for a bogus keyword at exception-collector's call site
reddened the suite at exit 1 with 1 failure whose assertion text named the
planted keyword, at the same 1903/7010 totals (so the plant crashed no namespace
and truncated no lane). The plant existed only in the worker worktree, so the
red is positive evidence the gate read this tree. Restored from HEAD, confirmed
by blob hash.

The local atom was correctly KEPT — the bead is explicit that these collectors capture exceptions arriving asynchronously from re-frame event-handler callbacks, a side-channel across time that cannot be threaded functionally through dispatch. The deliverable was deduplication, not functionalisation. No completion report (worker starved); close rests on the merged diff and a green rollup at band 87.

title: merge criterion: the clause-5 job-key discriminator counts job keys in workflows that have no pull_request trigger, so a nightly-only job reads as a check-set change
description:
FILED BY THE MAYOR 2026-09-05 from a live merge of PR #9277, where the discriminator read jobkeys=1 and the correct answer was "the PR check set did not change".

THE MECHANIC AS RECORDED. CLAUDE.md's trap (a) under the merge-criterion bullet gives the clause-5 discriminator as:

  git diff <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'

and the whole of that paragraph is about the TWO LEADING SPACES: the unindented form matches nothing, reads a reassuring zero, and fails OPEN. That half is right, is exercised in both directions, and is not what this bead is about.

WHAT IS MISSING. The discriminator counts job keys across EVERY file under .github/workflows/, but clause 5 is about the set of checks a PULL REQUEST will be graded on. A workflow with no `pull_request` trigger contributes no checks to any PR rollup, so a job added to one moves the count and not the band.

MEASURED, 2026-09-05, on PR #9277 (worker/specxray-a):
  merge-base b86310b3c1 .. origin/main  ->  wf=271  jobkeys=1
  the single key is `mcp-live-windows`, added to .github/workflows/expensive-tests.yml by PR #9276
  expensive-tests.yml `on:` is `schedule: cron "17 15 * * *"` + `workflow_dispatch` — no pull_request
  empirical corroboration: the band was 87 on the four PRs merged AFTER #9276 landed, and #9277's own rollup was 87

So the flag was real (the trunk's workflow tree did gain a job) and the inference it invites was wrong.

WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILS, because that decides the priority. This one fails CLOSED: it flags a merge that should proceed, where every other trap recorded in that bullet ADMITS a merge that should have been blocked. That makes it much less dangerous than its neighbours and is why this is P3 rather than P2. But it is not harmless, for two reasons: (i) it will fire on every nightly job addition, and a flag that is usually spurious trains the reader to wave it through, which is how a real one gets waved through too; (ii) the mayor that hit it verified the trigger AFTER merging rather than before, i.e. the recorded mechanic did not carry the check that discharges it — which is exactly the "hazard recorded without the test that discharges it" shape that loops.md §6 says to fix in the document.

THE REPAIR IS ONE CLAUSE, NOT A REWRITE. Trap (a) should say that a non-zero count is a question and not an answer, and name the question: read the `on:` block of the workflow file the key was added to, and count only keys in files carrying a `pull_request` trigger. The `+++ b/<path>` lines in the same diff already name the file, so the follow-up costs one command:

  git diff <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/ | grep -E '^(\+\+\+|\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$)'

DO NOT WEAKEN THE TWO-SPACE RULE OR THE FAIL-OPEN FRAMING while editing that paragraph. The paragraph's subject is three traps that each fail open; this addition is a qualification to (a), not a fourth trap, and it must not dilute the sentence that says a constant zero is the reassuring answer.

CHECK BEFORE ACTING, per the standing rule that this brief's premises are claims: re-read trap (a) at tip, confirm expensive-tests.yml still has no pull_request trigger, and confirm test.yml still keeps its pull_request trigger UNFILTERED (the phantom-pending trap rf2-dtvmb fixed) — the qualification must not read as licence to discount test.yml.

ALSO CONSIDER whether the same clause belongs in docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md §1 clause 5, which is the normative statement CLAUDE.md's bullet says it is not restating. If clause 5 already says "the trunk's current workflow matrix" in a way that covers this, the CLAUDE.md concretion is the only edit needed — say which and why.

SEQUENCING: CLAUDE.md is a hot file. rf2-u62e is live on it right now (worker hygiene-b, worktree C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2-worktrees/hygiene-b). This bead waits for that PR to merge. rf2-jwlh is also queued behind it.

title: http: an actor-destroy arriving inside the two-swap publication window fires nothing
description:
Residual measured while fixing rf2-o8ek's publication-race ghost.

registry/record-in-flight! publishes an actor-originated request to in-flight first and actor-in-flight second. At that MIDPOINT the request slot exists and the actor slot does not, so abort-on-actor-destroy walks the actor index, finds nothing, and fires nothing; publication then completes and the handle is fully live in BOTH indexes despite its actor having been destroyed.

Deterministic same-thread watch interleaving on tip (a watch on in-flight that calls (abort-on-actor-destroy :frame/a :actor/y) the instant the request slot appears) printed:

  {:case :actor-destroy-at-midpoint, :abort-fired? false, :request-slot-present? true, :actor-slot-count 1}

This is a MISSED abort, not an incoherent index — distinct from the ghost rf2-o8ek closed, which is why it was left. Severity is bounded: the orphan is still swept by the later frame-destroy / epoch-restore paths, and the window is the microseconds between two swap! calls on the JVM only (CLJS is single-threaded).

Reversing the publication order does not fix it, it only moves the blind door: with actor-in-flight published first, a :rf.http/managed-abort by request-id at the same midpoint would find nothing instead — and that is the primary app-facing cancellation verb, so the current order is the better of the two. A real fix needs publication to be observable as ONE step across both atoms (cross-atom atomicity), which is machinery this bead should weigh against the narrowness of the window before building.

Do not add a lock, a tombstone or a lease object without ruling that trade first.
notes:
WORKER OUTCOME (PR #9269, commit 5a3c24a543). Premise checked at source and CONFIRMED at tip: registry.cljc:197/199 are the two swaps, and record-in-flight!'s own docstring still declared the residual open. Reproduced deterministically with the EXISTING record-actor-handle-with-midpoint! harness in http_frame_scoped_cancellation_test.clj — abort never fired, request slot present, actor-slot-count 1, exactly as filed.

THE BEAD'S DESIGN PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD, and that is the substance of the fix. 'A real fix needs publication to be observable as ONE step across both atoms (cross-atom atomicity)' is false: record-in-flight! computes stamped-handle (carrying :frame AND :actor-id) BEFORE its first swap, so the copy in the request index at the midpoint already names its own actor. The destroy side simply had to read both indexes. No lock, no tombstone, no lease, no storage change, no publication-order change — so the 'weigh the machinery first' instruction was satisfied by finding there is no machinery to weigh. Both atoms and both keys are untouched.

Considered and rejected: collapsing the two atoms into one (the literal reading of 'one step across both atoms'). It works, but it is a rewrite of the registry's storage that would also make rf2-o8ek's two publication-window pins unable to reach their case and its reconcile dead code — a large change deleting another bead's shipped fix, for a P3 whose window is nanoseconds.

The frame filter on the new scan is load-bearing, not tidy: in-flight is keyed by request-id and holds every frame's work, so without it a destroy in frame A also aborts a sibling frame's identically-addressed actor. Pinned by actor-destroy-inside-the-publication-window-is-frame-exact; measured red when the filter is removed.

The two halves compose — aborting a midpoint handle drops its request slot, so rf2-o8ek's trailing reconcile then retracts the actor slot publication is about to write. No ghost either; asserted.

ALSO FIXED, same class, narrower door: abort-on-actor-destroy read the actor slot with get and cleared it with a separate swap!, so a handle published between the two was dissoc'd from the index unaborted — while the adjacent comment claimed the clear was atomic. Now one swap-vals!.

Gates (captured exits, final rebased base): implementation/http clojure -M:test exit 0, 527 tests / 3975 assertions (+2 tests over rf2-o8ek's 525 — the two added here); implementation/core exit 0, 2187/11320; implementation/resources exit 0, 829/7537. CLJS spine left to CI per dispatch fence (eight sibling workers live).

PREMISE CONFIRMED AT SOURCE: the two swaps are registry.cljc:197 (in-flight) and :199 (actor-in-flight), and record-in-flight!'s own docstring still declared the residual open — a hazard recorded without the test that discharges it. The window IS deterministically enterable: an existing harness (record-actor-handle-with-midpoint!) parks a writer there via an atom watch, which runs on the swapping thread before swap! returns. The filed measurement reproduced exactly.

THE BEAD'S OWN DESIGN PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD, AND THAT IS THE FIX. It reasoned that a real repair 'needs publication to be observable as ONE step across both atoms (cross-atom atomicity)'. It does not: record-in-flight! computes stamped-handle carrying :frame AND :actor-id BEFORE the first swap, so the request-index copy visible at the midpoint already names its actor. The handle was never invisible — only unlooked-for. abort-on-actor-destroy now reads both indexes. No lock, no tombstone, no cross-atom atomicity, no storage change, no publication-order change.
