**Status:** Medium-High (the validator-port setters have zero app/tool consumers across seven public names plus four dead facade wrappers; the boundary Var is a second public name for a value whose own docstring says "do not use me"; the rest is judgment; wave 3, 2026-09-05 09:05:36 AUSEST, tip 7d7ec09bd7)

**Surfaces:** `re-frame.schemas/set-schema-fns!` · `set-schema-validator!` · `set-schema-explainer!` · `set-schema-printer!` · `reset-schema-validator!` · `snapshot-schema-fns` · `restore-schema-fns!` (`implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validator.cljc:169-330`, re-exported `schemas.cljc:35-43`) · four dead `defwrapper`s in `re-frame.core-schemas` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/core_schemas.cljc:57-130`) and their four late-bind hooks (`late_bind/directory.cljc:362-377`) · `validate-at-boundary-interceptor` Var (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/spec.cljc:129`, facade `core.cljc:2048-2060`) and the `:rf.schema/at-boundary` interceptor id (`spec.cljc:316-341`) · `:schema` on `reg-event`/`reg-sub`/`reg-fx`/`reg-cofx`/`reg-flow` · `reg-app-schema` / `reg-app-schemas` · `reg-machine {:schemas {:data …}}` · `reg-resource`/`reg-mutation` `:params-schema` / `:data-schema` · `reg-route` `:params` / `:query` · `:rf.http/managed {:decode S}` · `reg-event {:rf.http/decode-schemas [S]}` · `{:sensitive? true}` slot props vs `:sensitive [[path]]` registration meta / commit-plane effect.

## The problem

**(a) The validator port.** The framework consults exactly three functions — `validate`, `explain`, `print` — held in three private atoms. Seven public names mutate or read them, and all seven lower to `reset!` on the same atoms:

| Spelling (tier) | Lowers to | Distinct job? |
|---|---|---|
| `(set-schema-fns! {:validate f :explain g :print h})` (advanced, "preferred") | partial `reset!` per present key; returns the full bundle | the door |
| `(set-schema-validator! f)` (advanced) | `(reset! validator-fn f)` | = `(set-schema-fns! {:validate f})` |
| `(set-schema-explainer! g)` (advanced) | `(reset! explainer-fn g)` | = `(set-schema-fns! {:explain g})` |
| `(set-schema-printer! h)` (advanced) | `(reset! printer-fn (or h default))` | = `(set-schema-fns! {:print h})` |
| `(reset-schema-validator!)` (advanced) | three `reset!`s to the Malli defaults | = `(set-schema-fns! <defaults>)` — but the defaults are private, so this is the only way to spell it |
| `(snapshot-schema-fns)` (implementation) | read the three atoms | the only read; a read named like a test helper |
| `(restore-schema-fns! bundle)` (implementation) | `(set-schema-fns! bundle)` — literally, `validator.cljc:330` | none |

Beneath those, `re-frame.core-schemas` still carries `defwrapper set-schema-validator!` / `set-schema-fns!` / `set-schema-explainer!` / `set-schema-printer!` (`core_schemas.cljc:57-130`) and `late_bind/directory.cljc:362-377` publishes four `:schemas/set-schema-*` hooks to serve them — but rf2-wad2fl removed the re-exports from `re-frame.core` (`core.cljc:1038-1047`), so the wrappers have **zero consumers anywhere** (`git grep -E "core-schemas/set-schema"` → nothing). `spec/Conventions.md:1436-1437` still teaches `(rf/set-schema-validator! malli.core/validate)`, a spelling that no longer resolves.

**(b) Saying "validate this value against a schema".** One key, `:schema`, plus six other spellings; the *meaning* of `:schema` — dev-only diagnostic or always-on guard — is decided per surface and spelled inconsistently:

| Spelling | Value checked | Build | On failure | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reg-event {:schema S}` | event vector | dev-only | skip handler, trace | `validate.cljc:1073` |
| `reg-event {:schema S :interceptors [:rf.schema/at-boundary]}` | event vector | **always** | skip handler, always-on `:errors` record | `spec.cljc:129-200`; spec/010 §Production builds |
| `reg-sub {:schema S}` / `reg-fx {:schema S}` / `reg-flow {:schema S}` | return / args / output | dev-only | nil / skip fx / observe | `validate.cljc:1117,1155`; `flows.cljc:109` |
| `reg-cofx {:schema S}` | recordable cofx value | **always** | throw `:rf.error/cofx-value-invalid` | `cofx.cljc:665-700` |

The discriminator for dev-only vs always-on IS written — C-000.35, "what the check is for, not who declared the schema it reads" (spec/010:210) — but it is not *visible in the spelling*: the same key `:schema` is a dev diagnostic on `reg-event` and a production hard error on `reg-cofx`, always-on checks are named `-schema` (`:params-schema`), bare (`:params`), and `:decode`, and two keys with `schema` in their name validate nothing. Production enforcement of an event schema is the one case with a *second public name*: the `:rf.schema/at-boundary` id (the only spelling any consumer uses) and the `validate-at-boundary-interceptor` Var, exported from two namespaces, whose spec row, facade docstring and API doc all say: do not call it, do not put it in a chain (spec/API.md:565; `core.cljc:2048-2059`). ## Simpler elegant target

**(a) The validator port is a value.** Three names replace seven public names, four dead wrappers and four late-bind hooks:

```clojure
;; re-frame.schemas
(def malli-schema-fns {:validate default-malli-validate   ; the default port, as a public VALUE
                       :explain  default-malli-explain
                       :print    default-edn-print})
(schema-fns)                                   ; → {:validate f :explain g :print h}   (read; no bang)
(set-schema-fns! {:validate f :explain g :print h})  ; partial or full install; returns the bundle
```

| Use case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| install a port | `(set-schema-fns! {…})` | unchanged |
| swap one fn | `(set-schema-validator! f)` | `(set-schema-fns! {:validate f})` |
| disable validation | `(set-schema-validator! nil)` | `(set-schema-fns! {:validate nil})` |
| reset to defaults | `(reset-schema-validator!)` | `(set-schema-fns! schemas/malli-schema-fns)` |
| capture / restore | `(let [s (snapshot-schema-fns)] … (finally (restore-schema-fns! s)))` | `(let [s (schema-fns)] … (finally (set-schema-fns! s)))` |

Delete: `set-schema-validator!`, `set-schema-explainer!`, `set-schema-printer!`, `reset-schema-validator!`, `snapshot-schema-fns`, `restore-schema-fns!` (six names); the four `defwrapper`s in `core_schemas.cljc:57-130`; the four `:schemas/set-schema-*` hooks in `directory.cljc:362-377` and their `late-bind/set-fn!` lines in `schemas.cljc:134-137`. The `:print nil → default` coercion stays inside `set-schema-fns!` (it already is).

**(b) Production enforcement is a property of the schema, not a chain step.** The registrar already treats it that way: it rejects the interceptor without a `:schema` (`events.cljc:235-263`), ignores a per-frame chain that attaches it (`events.cljc:265-284`), scans the authored chain for a keyword to find it (`events.cljc:202-222`), special-cases the `[:rf.schema/at-boundary arg]` 2-vector (`events.cljc:207-216`), and must re-register the interceptor after every `clear-all!` (`spec.cljc:311-345`; `core.cljc:2693`). Five pieces of machinery to make a chain entry behave like a flag. Make it a flag:

```clojure
(rf/reg-event :ws/handle-message
  {:schema    [:cat [:= :ws/handle-message] InboundMessage]
   :boundary? true}                      ; "this :schema runs in every build"
  (fn [m] …))
```

`:boundary? true` without `:schema` stays `:rf.error/at-boundary-missing-schema` (a map lookup, not a chain scan). The `:before` fn in `spec.cljc:158-200` becomes the router's step-1 path when the flag is set, ungated. Delete: `validate-at-boundary-interceptor` (both homes), `register-schema-interceptors!`, the `:interceptor`-kind registration, `attaches-validate-at-boundary-interceptor?` / `boundary-guarded-handler?` chain scans, and the `:rf.schema/at-boundary` member of the reserved namespace (`spec/Conventions.md:117` — the closed set shrinks to `:rf.schema/violation`). **Floor if the flag is refused:** delete the Var alone — zero consumers, EP-0022 already says so, and the id keeps working unchanged.

**(c) One registrar per kind.** Delete `reg-app-schemas`; the three call sites become `(doseq [[p s] app-db-schemas] (rf/reg-app-schema p s))`. The atomic-batch guarantee (`:rf.error/app-schemas-bad-batch`, spec/010:115) protects against a registration-time typo the singular already rejects per entry.

**(d) One reflective key, honestly named.** Delete resource `:data-schema` (8 sites, one consumer at `tooling.cljc:239`) and declare the decoded shape the same way an event handler does — `:rf.http/decode-schemas [S]` on the resource's metadata — so a tool reads one key on both registrars and nobody reads `-schema` as "validates".

**Not proposed:** collapsing `:params-schema` / `:params` / `:decode` / cofx `:schema` into one word. Each is on a different registrar with a different value slot, and each is always-on because of what it guards. What (b) fixes is the one surface where the same key `:schema` flips meaning by adding an interceptor.

## Why this is better (ethos)


- **Regularity over cleverness (Principles.md:18).** "There is one obvious way to do a thing." Seven names for three atoms is six ways too many, and the API doc already spends three rows saying "prefer the other one" (spec/API.md:562-564). A port that is a *value* — install it, read it, `let`-bind it — needs no reset, snapshot or restore verbs; those are Clojure's `def` and `let`. `reset-schema-validator!` exists only because the default is hidden; publish the default and the verb disappears.
- **Data before magic (Principles.md:46).** A chain entry whose presence the registrar must *scan for*, whose absence of `:schema` is an error, and which a per-frame chain is forbidden to add, is not behaving as an interceptor — it is a boolean wearing an interceptor's clothes. `handler-meta` should answer "is this handler boundary-guarded?" by reading a key, not by parsing a chain (`events.cljc:265-284` does exactly that parse today, on every refusal).
- **Shapes are describable (Principles.md:58).** The schema is the description; *when it is enforced* is a property of that description. Putting the build-mode next to the schema (`:schema` + `:boundary?`) keeps the two facts adjacent and queryable; putting one in `:schema` and the other in `:interceptors` scatters one decision across two keys.
- **Trust the programmer.** `(set-schema-fns! {:validate nil})` already says "off"; a second verb that says it again is a nag, not a feature.
- **Clojure ethos.** Configuration as a map, defaults as a public value, mutation through one bang verb and reads through its no-bang twin — this is the `configure!` / `current-config` law Conventions.md:1277 already lays down for bucket 1; bucket 2 should obey the same shape.
- **Honest costs.** (a) Six deletions ripple through ~12 test files (mechanical). (b) rewrites the 2 example sites, 29 doc lines, 42 skill lines and the improver evals that teach `:rf.schema/at-boundary`; the interceptor form is the EP-0022-regular way to attach cross-cutting behaviour, and a reader who already knows `:rf.interceptor/path` gets it for free — the flag trades that regularity for a smaller mechanism. (c) loses per-entry source-coords precision (a `doseq` stamps one line) and the bulk shape spec/010:104 recommends for feature modules. (d) is 8 call sites and a rename.

# Schema backend configuration: one partial-map installer

Review date: 2026-09-05. Status: proposal only. Tracking bead: `rf2-snkw`.

## Finding

[re-frame.schemas](../../../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas.cljc) exposes `set-schema-fns!`, `set-schema-validator!`, `set-schema-explainer!`, `set-schema-printer!`, and `reset-schema-validator!`.


The first already accepts any subset of the three backend functions. The next three independently write the same slots. The last name sounds validator-specific but resets all three functions; its implementation explicitly describes it as test support.

[The validator implementation](../../../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validator.cljc), at these definitions, establishes the overlap directly:

| Current operation | Equivalent installation through the existing bundle API |
| --- | --- |
| `(set-schema-validator! v)` | `(set-schema-fns! {:validate v})` |
| `(set-schema-explainer! e)` | `(set-schema-fns! {:explain e})` |
| `(set-schema-printer! p)` | `(set-schema-fns! {:print p})` |

The write semantics are equivalent, but returns differ: a scalar setter returns its installed function, whereas the bundle setter returns the full installed bundle. That difference matters to migration; it is not evidence of a different configuration capability.

## Known use cases and empirical evidence

| Use case | Repository evidence | Requirement to retain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary application schema registration using the default backend | [RealWorld HTTP schemas](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_http/schema.cljs), [resource schemas](../../../../examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/schema.cljs) | No backend setup ceremony is required. Registering app schemas remains separate from replacing the schema engine. |
| Install a non-default validator/explainer/printer together | `set-schema-fns!` implementation and [printer seam tests](../../../../implementation/schemas/test/re_frame/schemas/printer_seam_test.clj) | One map can replace all three cooperating functions. |
| Change only validation, explanation, or printing | Scalar setter implementations and printer seam tests | Omitted bundle keys retain their prior values. A partial map already serves this case. |
| Deliberately disable validation | [Production boundary tests](../../../../implementation/schemas/test/re_frame/schemas_boundary_prod_test.cljs), [bundle probe](../../../../implementation/schemas/test/re_frame/schemas_bundle_probe.cljs) | Explicit `:validate nil` keeps its supported opt-out meaning. |
| Disable explanations without disabling validation | Validator implementation's explainer contract | `:explain nil` is distinct from omission. |
| Reset the printer to deterministic EDN rendering | Printer seam tests, including nil-printer cases | `:print nil` installs the default printer; it does not leave an undefined digest representation. |
| Inspect what was installed, including untouched slots | Printer seam tests of the bundle return | Return the full installed map, including default-printer coercion. |
| Restore test isolation after temporary changes | `snapshot-schema-fns`, `restore-schema-fns!`, `reset-schema-validator!` in the validator implementation | Restore all relevant state reliably; a test fixture is not an application boot API. |
| Stable schema digests and tool inspection | [Schema digest implementation](../../../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/digest.cljc), [Xray schemas panel](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/static/schemas/panel.cljs) | Keep deterministic printing/digests and frame-local schema visibility; neither requires separate installation verbs. |

The authored examples/tools searches found no direct calls to these backend setters. The demonstrated application path uses default installation and schema registration; custom backend configuration is supported chiefly by implementation contracts and tests in this repository. That makes this a modest surface cleanup, not a claim that everyday apps are suffering from all four setters.

## Proposed smaller API

Keep the already-existing `set-schema-fns!` name and semantics as the sole public application installation operation:

```clojure
;; All supported today; proposed as the only backend-installation vocabulary.
(schemas/set-schema-fns! {:validate my-validator})
(schemas/set-schema-fns! {:explain my-explainer :print my-printer})
(schemas/set-schema-fns! {:validate nil})
```

Remove the three scalar setters from the supported authoring surface. Do not replace them with `install!`, `configure!`, `with-backend`, per-frame backend policies, or a new plugin registry. The useful abstraction already exists.

Preserve the current distinction between omitted and explicit-nil keys. Preserve the full bundle return. If a caller uses a scalar setter's return, it can explicitly select the corresponding key from the bundle result. This is especially important for `:print nil`, whose returned installed value is the default printer, not nil.

Treat default reset and snapshot/restore as fixture facilities. The existing internal restoration helper already delegates to the bundle installer. Keep that encapsulation for tests; remove the misleading validator-only reset name from the application configuration story. Prefer restoring the fixture's captured prior bundle when that is the intended isolation boundary, rather than assuming every test began with framework defaults.

This is a public-surface reduction, not a demand to combine the three internal atoms. Configuration is currently a quiescent boot/fixture operation; the implementation explicitly says snapshots are not transactional. Do not describe the existing bundle install as an atomic transaction, and do not invent concurrency machinery without a caller that needs it.

## Counterargument and boundaries

A dedicated setter has an immediately recognizable name and returns exactly the value it installs. For a one-line REPL experiment it saves a map. The partial-map installer costs a little punctuation, but already has to be learned for installing a coherent custom backend. Three extra names, separate return contracts and repeated nil semantics do not buy a distinct use case.

Do not extend this argument to deleting `reg-app-schemas`. Its callers in both RealWorld applications supply meaningful path-to-schema maps, and the bulk registration path validates inputs before applying them. It is not interchangeable with an arbitrary loop of single registrations. Nor should app-schema collections, schema hashes or frame selection be folded into backend installation; those are different data and lifetimes.

## Why this is more elegant

A schema backend is three cooperating functions. An ordinary map expresses that relationship directly, and Clojure's partial-map update idiom naturally expresses changing just one part. The programmer supplies values without needing a vocabulary of setters proportional to the number of fields.

This aligns with [Vision](../../../../spec/000-Vision.md) and [Principles](../../../../spec/Principles.md): data-oriented composition, regularity, optional schema policy, and low hidden ceremony. Trusting the programmer means preserving custom functions and explicit opt-out, not introducing new validation policies while tidying names.

## Focused acceptance evidence

Migrate the setter tests to the bundle operation while retaining coverage of omitted versus nil keys, default printer coercion, full bundle returns, custom-validator boundary behavior, digest stability and complete fixture restoration. Check any higher-order or return-value-dependent callers before removing exports. No application runtime behavior, schema language, or digest algorithm needs to change.

## Follow-on comparison with Fable

[Fable's schema](../fable/schema-configuration-and-validation.md) and [registration](../fable/registration-spellings.md) reviews corroborate the bundle-setter reduction. I do not adopt their `reg-app-schemas` deletion as written: [storage's implementation](../../../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/storage.cljc) checks the batch and every path before applying any registration, then returns a vector of paths. Replacing it with the proposed `run!` loses both that up-front validation behavior and the return contract. Keeping this small, useful bulk operation better serves the stated ergonomics posture than making each application reconstruct it.

On the second reread, both Fable documents' later cross-check sections explicitly withdraw that deletion and retain the bulk API. This is now agreement, not an outstanding disagreement; some earlier summary rows still show the old proposal. The guarantee is specifically up-front shape/path validation, not transactional rollback for every possible failure later in registration.

## The problem

### What exists today

A `reg-event` `:schema` is a dev-only diagnostic: `validate-event!` sits behind `(if interop/debug-enabled? …)` (`implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc:1148,1172`) and a release build never runs it. To keep the check in production a handler references a framework-registered interceptor by id. The websocket example is the only app code that does this (both sites in one file):

```clojure
;; examples/patterns/websocket/messages.cljs:494-505 (second site: :585-586)
(rf/reg-event :ws/handle-message
  {:doc          "Fold one inbound frame into app-db. UNTRUSTED INGRESS — …"
   :schema       [:cat [:= :ws/handle-message] schema/InboundMessage]
   :interceptors [:rf.schema/at-boundary]}
  (fn handler-ws-handle-message [{:keys [db]} [_ body]] …))
```

Twelve lines of comment above it (`:476-493`) exist to explain the second key: "`:rf.schema/at-boundary` is what keeps the check in the RELEASE build (a bare `:schema` is a dev diagnostic and elides under :advanced)". The how-to teaches the same shape (`docs/core/how-to/validate-with-schemas.md:339-344`) and then spends a paragraph on what the entry is *not*: not a second schema, not usable without `:schema`, not the Var.

Under Option A the same registration reads:

```clojure
(rf/reg-event :ws/handle-message
  {:doc      "…"
   :schema   [:cat [:= :ws/handle-message] schema/InboundMessage]
   :boundary? true}                     ; this :schema runs in every build
  (fn handler-ws-handle-message [{:keys [db]} [_ body]] …))
```

Three facts, each verified at tip, show the chain entry is a boolean wearing an interceptor's clothes:

1. **It does nothing in dev and something in prod.** The `:before` fn returns `ctx` untouched when `(dev-mode?)` (`spec.cljc:160-166`); step-1 `validate-event!` (`router.cljc:790,3076`) does the refusing there. Only in a release build does the interceptor's own body run.

3. **`:interceptor-overrides` reaches it in one build only.** `{:rf.schema/at-boundary nil}` removes the chain entry (`router.cljc:2408-2412`), so in prod it removes the check; in dev step-1 still refuses and mechanism 3 still stamps `:rf/boundary-rejected?` because it reads the authored chain, not the effective one. ## Codex Recommendation

Choose **A: `{:schema S :boundary? true}`**, with one precise contract: check the original dispatched event against the already-resolved handler's schema once, before executing its interceptor chain, in every build. This makes a useful policy directly readable on the registration and removes a real development/production inconsistency. Keep ordinary schema diagnostics, other registrars' schema meanings, and resource `:data-schema` as designed. Delete the old opt-in and public interceptor value without a compatibility alias.

Independent review at source SHA `436e2b062afed4041d688d11617005a31b4f7157`; tool time **2026-09-06 06:49:41 UTC**. I read the complete decision and the associated bead's JSON description (16,767 characters), notes (42,155 characters), acceptance criteria and status. `rf2-kuky.40` remains **open**, and the proposed flag has **not landed**: [registration keys](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/reg_meta.cljc) still omit it, while the interceptor registration, facade export and boot re-seeding remain. Related `.39`, `.41` and `.13` are open; `rf2-xpd8`, `rf2-vkn8` and `rf2-51in` are closed.

The decisive evidence is behavioral:

- [The router](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc), at `validate-event!`, `prepare-handler-ctx` and `run-chain`, validates the original event in development, then executes the resolved and overridden chain. [The production interceptor](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/spec.cljc) instead reads the chain's current `:event`. It also derives a fresh event id and looks up metadata from that value. Consequently, an earlier interceptor changing the event id can select a different schema, or no matching metadata, while the router still executes the originally selected handler. Passing the router's resolved metadata into the new boundary check avoids both discrepancies.
- [Registration](../../implementation/core/src/re_frame/events.cljc) already binds the opt-in to a handler's own schema declaration. Its missing-schema test and development rejection marker inspect authored references; production execution honors overrides and frame-added references. These are genuine chain semantics, but they do not provide one consistent validation policy across builds.

The implementation should preserve the current step-1 location and recovery, not create an earlier dispatch subsystem. `run-chain` intentionally executes interceptors after a validation refusal so their `:after` cleanup still runs. Set the skip and boundary-rejection markers; retain the existing tail emission, downstream drain and frame-owner liveness checks. Callback code can destroy a frame during validation or explanation, so preserve the continuation checks already present in [schema validation](../../implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc). Do not route the new always-on branch through the router helper's existing catch-and-pass fallback: validator failure must remain a rejection, while an explainer failure must not reverse that verdict.

Keep the optional backend contract: no schemas artefact or an explicitly disabled validator means no validation. A present `:schema nil` or `false` remains an opaque token delegated to the backend; only an absent schema key triggers the registration error. Use the same boolean predicate for registration, enforcement and rejection attribution. Share the decision point without retaining every dev diagnostic in production: the existing dev validation and ungated backend seams can remain distinct internally.

The consumer evidence supports this scope. Searches across application and tool Clojure sources found exactly two attachments, both in [websocket messages](../../examples/patterns/websocket/messages.cljs), and no tool reference to the boundary id. Story and pair-MCP use general interceptor overrides, which remain useful independently. This is a small application migration with a substantial teaching migration. In particular, preserve the [improver's event-payload/body-read distinction](../../skills/re-frame2-improver/references/schemaless-events.md): the flag does not validate a value first read inside the handler. Its existing regression examples must continue to reject that mistaken inference.

The strongest alternative is **B**. An interceptor offers deliberate placement after decoding or normalization and can be substituted for a scenario; removing its public Var alone avoids the teaching rewrite while retaining those capabilities. That is a sound choice if programmable validation placement is the intended contract. However, the shipped dev path already validates before such transformations, and the inspected consumers need input enforcement. A therefore delivers a more predictable contract. Authors needing a different, explicitly ordered check can still register an application interceptor. **C** retains a value the public reference-only grammar does not consume and whose retirement [EP-0022](../../docs/EP/EP-0022-registered-interceptors.md) already anticipates. **D** is workable but has no demonstrated third mode to justify an enum. Neither a schema wrapper nor a new policy framework improves this narrow decision.

Ship one coherent implementation change after coordinating `.39`'s shared files: add the event metadata key and schema row; replace detection with the flag; remove the ref, Var, registration and re-seed hook; update manifests, specifications, migration M-59, examples, docs, skills and eval fixtures together. Retain the missing-schema check as a simpler lookup. Resource reflection has actual consumers in [resource tooling](../../implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/tooling.cljc) and Xray; it is a distinct capability, not a duplicate enforcement spelling.

Focused checks should count validator calls and pin original-value/original-schema selection with a transforming interceptor, plus overrides, in dev and production. Preserve nil-token delegation, disabled-backend behavior, throwing validators/explainers, cleanup, one structural rejection record, and SSR's 400 projection. Run the existing [advanced production suite](../../implementation/schemas/test/re_frame/schemas_boundary_prod_test.cljs), its dev counterpart, relevant SSR tests and bundle-elision checks; a JVM redefinition alone cannot establish Closure behavior. This review ran no builds or tests and did not reproduce the transformation scenario at runtime. The behavioral conclusions above are source-derived; historical corpus totals and worker-day estimates were not independently remeasured.

title: check_doc_slugs.py polices skills/ but no PR-time job runs it on a skills-only change — rf2-6ng7 class, the twin of the inject-cofx fix
description:
Found by the rf2-skvce tree-claim meta-check while writing the declared list's reason strings.

THE DEFECT. scripts/check_doc_slugs.py's DEFAULT_ROOTS is docs, spec, skills, migration (plus tools/*/spec). It runs in exactly one PR-time place: docs.yml's 'build' job, which is gated on that workflow's docs_surface classifier. That classifier's case list is docs/*|spec/*|migration/*|mkdocs.yml|mkdocs_hooks.py|TESTING.md|README.md|CHANGELOG.md|SKILL-REDIRECT.md|AGENTS.md|CLAUDE.md|...|testbeds/*|tools/*/spec/*|.github/workflows/docs.yml — and skills/* is NOT on it. Measured: a skills-only path lights docs_surface false and arms zero outputs in test.yml's classifier too.

So one of the gate's four scan roots sits outside its own arming. A skills/**/*.md PR that plants a broken markdown link target or a dangling heading anchor runs the slug validator NOWHERE at PR time. (test.yml's push filter also paths-ignores 'skills/**/*.md', so the post-merge run does not catch it either; scripts/test-fast-pr.sh does run it, but a local spine is not a mechanism.)

THIS IS THE EXACT DEFECT test.yml:713-724 ALREADY NAMES AND FIXED ONE GATE OVER. rf2-6ng7 moved scripts/check_inject_cofx_residue.py out of docs.yml's build job for this very reason — 'a case list carrying docs/*, spec/*, migration/*, testbeds/* and a dozen named files, but NOT skills/*. One of the gate's four scan roots was therefore outside its own arming.' The remedy chosen there was explicitly NOT a wider docs_surface (that buys a ~15-minute MkDocs build on every skills PR) but 'no surface at all' — relocating the sub-second pure-stdlib check into test.yml's always-on 'Repo invariant checks' job. check_doc_slugs.py has the same shape (pure Python, self-testable via --self-test) and the same three other roots.

WHAT THE FIXER MUST CHECK BEFORE COPYING THAT REMEDY. check_doc_slugs.py is 2300+ lines and considerably heavier than the inject-cofx residue scan; measure its wall clock over the full corpus first. If it is cheap, the always-on job is the answer and docs.yml's copy retires. If it is not, the alternatives are (a) a skills-only invocation in the always-on job with the full corpus staying in docs.yml, or (b) adding skills/* to docs_surface and accepting the MkDocs cost, which test.yml:721 already argues against.

NOT A DUPLICATE of the arming half: skills/re-frame2-pair/*, skills/shared/* and skills/re-frame2-setup/* DO arm skills_structural, and the prose skill trees ARE reached by the always-on verify-skill-mcp-drift job (check_skill_mcp_drift.py + check_inject_cofx_residue.py). What no PR-time job reaches is the SLUG/ANCHOR validation of skills markdown.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #8197. Premise VERIFIED at source: docs_surface's case list, evaluated verbatim against skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md, returns false; check_doc_slugs.py is invoked by run: in exactly two places, both in docs.yml's docs_surface-gated build job. 176 skills markdown files were unvalidated at PR time.

ONE PREMISE REFUTED. The bead proposed test.yml's always-on verify-skill-mcp-drift job on the grounds that this gate is 'pure Python, self-testable' like check_inject_cofx_residue.py. It is NOT pure stdlib: check_doc_slugs.py:76-84 hard-requires pymdown-extensions and exits 2 without it. That job has no pip install, so the literal remedy would have redded every PR. Landed in verify-readme-links instead — unconditional, already installs requirements.txt for the same slugifier, and is this gate's declared companion (check_readme_links.py imports SLUGIFY from it).

SAYS-WHAT-IT-INSPECTED shipped too — --verbose now prints per-root file counts (docs 400 / spec 60 / skills 176 / migration 8 / seven tools/*/spec), so reach is on the page beside the verdict and a root dropping out of scope shows as a 0. Four documents claiming the gate runs in docs.yml (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, TESTING.md, docs/AUTHORING.md) corrected in the same patch.

comments.text:
CORRECTS SOMETHING I HAVE BEEN PUTTING IN BRIEFS ALL SESSION (mayor, 2026-08-14). I have told workers that check_doc_slugs.py's roster is docs, spec, skills, migration plus tools/*/spec, as shorthand for what it covers. That is accurate about the ROSTER and misleading about COVERAGE: the script runs only inside docs.yml's build job, gated on docs_surface, which excludes skills/*. A worker editing skills markdown who nominates this gate gets a green that means nothing.

THAT IS THE SAME VACUOUS-PASS SHAPE AS rf2-qfrrp, where check_provenance_pins run before committing inspects zero files and exits 0. Two gates, same failure: a pass that is indistinguishable from a real one because the gate is silent on success.

THE REMEDY IS KNOWN AND SMALL. test.yml lines 713-724 already solved this exact shape for check_inject_cofx_residue.py — that is the pattern to copy rather than design something new.

VERIFY BEFORE FIXING: confirm at source that docs_surface really excludes skills/*, and that no OTHER workflow runs check_doc_slugs.py on a skills path. The premise is a claim, and a sibling claim of this shape was refuted at source today when an exclusion pattern turned out not to match the namespace it was thought to exclude.

THE GENERAL LESSON WORTH CARRYING INTO THE FIX: a gate's ROSTER, its SCHEDULE and its REACH are three different things. This is the third instance today where quoting one as though it settled the others manufactured false confidence — the others being the provenance gate's vacuous green on uncommitted work, and the same gate absorbing a plant placed beside a landed pin. If the fix can make the gate SAY which trees it actually inspected on a run, that closes the whole family rather than this instance.

# hic-064 — FINAL CHECKPOINT: the §13 definition-of-done audit

**Phase**: 6 exit · **Wave**: G · **Est.**: L · **Depends**: hic-019, hic-026, hic-038, hic-048, hic-050, hic-060, hic-061, hic-062, hic-066, hic-068, hic-069, hic-071, hic-072 (re-runs the naming-ledger completeness grep — no provisional name ships)
**Surface**: read-only + final report + corrective bead files

## Goal
The independent, adversarial audit of every synth-codex §13 bullet — completeness, correctness, and quality assessed separately, by a fresh reviewer who trusts artifacts over claims.

## Review protocol
1. **Completeness**: §13 bullet by bullet, **verbatim from the spec** — package independence, small coherent language with no mode switch, explicit substrate/two-hook choices with the byte-exact shell disposition, full correctness matrix with sabotage controls, public-surface-only witnesses (incl. the hic-078 editor/grid), React-interop contract, per-surface SSR/hydration, ratified budgets met via the hic-071 reconciliation table (no silent breach rows), qualified bulk dispositions per hic-036, the warm-allocation non-claim (hic-072), native island parity vs both controls, testing ladder with honest opacity, Xray causal + privacy + erasure, every use case assigned, requirements mine + per-keystroke current, resource-demand verdict explicit (hic-050), donor independence (hic-062/076).
2. **Correctness**: clean-checkout full-suite run; re-run one sabotage per checkpoint domain (kernel, slice, native, coverage) plus the naming-census and erasure positive controls; verify the budgets reconciliation against a fresh pinned run on the physical reference profile.
3. **Quality**: the hic-069 fresh-reader result reviewed; three randomly chosen complaint ids traced id → docs anchor → recovery; the anti-cathedral check — list anything that grew beyond its witness.

## Green definition and output
**Green** = every §13 bullet green AND zero unresolved correctness/coverage rows in the hic-073 correction ledger. Anything else is a **non-release verdict** with the misses enumerated. The audit distinguishes two states explicitly: *implementation audit complete* (achievable without pilots) and *product definition of done* (red until hic-063 supplies two pilots — say so plainly). Output: `docs/design/hicasso/product/definition-of-done-audit.md` with per-bullet verdicts and the filed correction ids. Thresholds never widen to turn a bullet green.

---
[Worker context — applies to every hic bead]
PATH MAP: the normative documents are published in-tree by bead rf2-hic-000:
- docs/design/hicasso/product/decision-brief.md  (= synth.md / "the decision brief")
- docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md   (= "spec SN" / synth-codex.md)
- docs/design/hicasso/product/lanes/<name>.md    (= codex/<name>.md)
References to `fable/...` are operator-local provenance; workers do not need them.
PROPOSED-ID MAP: "hic-NNN" in any bead text = tracker id rf2-hic-NNN. The dependency manifest is authoritative over prose Depends lines.
WORKER PROTOCOL (mandatory):
1. Run the worker worktree guard before edits: sh scripts/assert-worker-worktree.sh; report WORKTREE_ROOT.
2. Read first: the path-mapped documents this bead names.
3. Gates: foreground a gate that fits inside the harness ceiling; DETACH one that does not and poll BOTH its log and its `.exit` file in a bounded loop within the same turn — never end the turn waiting for a completion event. Never pipe a gate through `tail` or any filter; redirect to a log and echo the runner's own exit code on the same command line. Commit and open the PR before ending the turn. DOC-SURFACE GATE: for an edit confined to docs/design/hicasso/, `mkdocs build --strict` is NOT the gate — mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs keeps that tree out of the site. `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` validates its markdown link targets and heading anchors, and `scripts/check_provenance_pins.py` validates changed pages under docs/design/hicasso/; nothing validates its tables, rendering or nav, so verify anchors and table column counts BY HAND and say so in the PR body.
4. Never `git stash`. Commit first, then rebase.
5. Never commit `.beads/issues.jsonl` or `.beads/metadata.json` from a worker branch — they are whole-database EXPORTS, not database files, and your branch carries the snapshot taken when its worktree was created, so committing one TIME-TRAVELS the tracker: beads closed since reopen, beads filed since vanish (PR #6677 did exactly this, 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral). Any other database-derived path likewise. The human-authored config — `.beads/README.md`, `.beads/config.yaml`, `.beads/.gitignore`, `.beads/hooks/**` — IS fair game. CLAUDE.md's Beads durability section is the authority.
6. Beads touching tools/xray/ update tools/xray/spec/* in the same PR (or state "spec unchanged because X").
7. Hot-zone files only if this bead flags them — and the hot zone INCLUDES the spec/*.md hot files (spec/004-Views.md, spec/002-Frames.md, spec/API.md, spec/Conventions.md among others), not just implementation/shadow-cljs.edn, implementation/deps.edn and .github/workflows/*. CLAUDE.md's Workflow section carries the canonical list; read it there rather than treating this line as complete.
8. No AI attribution in commits or PRs.
9. If you created a node_modules junction, remove it as your last act.
10. Checkpoint findings become real bd issues AND a row in docs/design/hicasso/product/correction-ledger.md. The checkpoint's own report PR writes the `open` row; a CORRECTIVE PR never edits that file — every later transition is the ledger keeper's. Read the file's own stated protocol before touching it.

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: tools/story top-level story_* files
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: tools/story top-level story_* files. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.6 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.6 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.6 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.6) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under tools/story top-level story_* files. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/story top-level story_* files. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/story top-level story_* files to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/story top-level story_* files; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/story top-level story_* files plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/story top-level story_* files that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: story run-owner: superseded-resume-never-greens-and-never-reads-successor flaked once, reading :pass and firing two effects (possible supersession race)
description:
A FLAKE THAT MAY BE A REAL RACE, reported by the fifth-pass pruning of tools/story play/ (rf2-nvxtm.8, PR #11181). The test's own name says a superseded resume must never green and never read its successor. A run that reads :pass and fires effects is therefore exactly the behaviour it exists to forbid. Treat this as a possible race in the run-owner's supersession logic, not as test noise.

Do not delete or weaken the test.

than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

implementation/flows to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:

   runner actually executes each file in implementation/flows; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.

   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.

   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.

  caller passes and the contract does not mention.

  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.

  drop the mid-range ones.

  resting a deletion on it.

  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/flows that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside <DIR> that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

Unit tests only. Gate-shaped harnesses are out: e2e, acceptance, feature-matrix, live and integration harnesses, and the docs playground smoke. The three tiny surfaces the third pass left without a child (the docs pilot tests, implementation/spec-resource, and the skills/reagent-migration and skills/re-frame2 fixtures) stay out.

A test cited by name in a spec, a doc, another test, a workflow or a roster stays unless the citation moves in the same change. A citation in a dated, commit-pinned findings snapshot does not keep a test (the rf2-n6gq4 RULING of 2026-10-05); list such names in the PR body.

Before deleting a test, check whether a fourth-pass close reason or notes (rf2-txsk5 and rf2-txsk5.1 to .46), a third-pass close reason (rf2-n6gq4.1 to .38), or this epic's notes name it as another surface's cover. If one does, it stays unless you name another surviving cover and prove it with a plant. Then, as the branch's last commit and in a commit of its own, lower the floor by exactly the number of tests your branch removed from that gate's lane, starting from the floor's value on trunk, and give the before and after counts in the message. Never lower a floor without deletions beside it. Several children share one floor line (the five core children share scripts/test-core-prod-gate.sh), so that line conflicts on rebase by design. On a conflict there, take trunk's value and subtract your own removal count again.

- the shadow-cljs lane. JVM lanes run freely. CLJS counts come from your PR's CI: the whole-lane :node-test and :browser-test deltas against main's run at your merge base. A CLJS-only deletion may rest on a structural argument: a kept test drives the same code path with an equal or stronger assertion. Say "structural" and name that test. Where a CLJS plant is genuinely needed, finish everything else first, ask the coordinator for the lane once, and run all such plants in that one window. Never run a shadow-cljs build without a grant (AGENTS.md).
- Plants. Never commit or push a plant. After each, restore the file and confirm it matches the committed blob (`git diff --quiet HEAD -- <path>`).
- Parallel. Children run in parallel, because each owns one surface's test files plus at most its own gate's floor line. A child that would touch another surface's tests stops and tells the coordinator.
- One worktree and one PR per child, opened as a draft and marked ready as the last act. Production code untouched. No .beads paths and no AI attribution in commits or the PR (CLAUDE.md).
- The report goes in the PR body, with a `## Quality gates` section, and as a summary appended to the child's notes (`bd update --append-notes`, from a file, never `--notes`). The worker does not close its child; the mayor closes it when the PR merges.

title: Fresco forms guide reverses the render-time revision fence for Enter and blur intents
description:
Found in merged PR #11153 (4ca14145b56091ae9010fb81e3873c8555a74fe0); the sentence remains on current main.

The new paragraph after :todo/title-replaced in docs/core/fresco/05-forms.md says that after the next render the draft's Enter and blur intents carry the OLD revision and therefore commit nothing. The protocol does the opposite: the old draft record retains its old revision, callbacks from the next render carry the NEW prop revision, and that mismatch refuses them. A previously captured intent carrying the OLD revision can still match and commit that record.

Evidence: implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/forms.cljs, ::commit lines 139-152, states the rendered fence and saved-intent limit. implementation/fresco/test/re_frame/fresco/forms_cljs_test.cljs/the-fence-is-the-render-and-that-limit-is-stated (lines 360-388 at this merge) deliberately asserts that type at revision 0, settle, then an old revision-0 commit still commits the old draft. docs/api/re-frame.fresco.forms.md already states this limit accurately.

Small correction: say that Enter/blur callbacks from the next render carry the NEW revision and cannot commit the previous draft, and retain the distinction for an intent captured before the reset rendered. This is a prose correction only; keep the existing protocol and regression unchanged. Do not add a stronger runtime fence or new state.

Acceptance: the forms chapter agrees with the commit handler, the existing saved-intent regression and API reference about which revision is refused.

DISPATCH 2026-10-15 17:54 AUSEST (mayor): dispatched to a background worker in worktree re-frame2-worktrees/fresco-forms-fence (branch worker/fresco-forms-fence, base f6a03b56aa). The sentence is still on trunk at docs/core/fresco/05-forms.md l.167. Prose only.
WORKER 2026-10-15 18:03 AUSEST (fresco-forms-fence): prose fix on PR #11249, awaiting merge. Claim verified at source at f6a03b56aa:
- forms.cljs `::commit` docstring: "A commit produced after a reset render carries the new revision and is refused; an intent captured BEFORE that render and delivered after it is indistinguishable from an ordinary commit and commits." The handler refuses any record that is not `live?` under the carried revision.

title: Spec 014's search example teaches an abort that sends a :cancelled reply per keystroke; two HTTP spec sentences name things that do not exist
description:

title: Reload sweep leaves deleted subscriptions live in the cache
description:
Found while auditing merged PR #11240 (f58f426632011939c2906cef427eda0c3a06ee8b). The sweep deletes a subscription's registration but does not invalidate its live cached reaction, so deleting the reg-sub form under hot reload can leave the application running that deleted computation.

At the merge, implementation/core/src/re_frame/registrar.cljc:1020 forget-stale-registration! reaches unregister! (:891) for the last provenance leaf. That removes the registrar/source-store entry and marks image reprojection dirty. A frame made without :images has no generation to reproject. The sub-cache replacement hook in implementation/core/src/re_frame/subs/cache.cljc:449 fires only on registration replacement; this removal triggers neither that hook nor invalidate-frame-subs!.

Confirmed with a plain-atom JVM probe on current main, using public make-frame and subscribe, and the real begin/sweep hooks (exit 0; no shadow-cljs run):
1. Register :audit/value as (fn [db _] (:n db)) and :audit/keep in namespace audit.reload; make :audit/live without :images; seed :n to 1 and hold the subscription.
2. Begin a reload cycle, register only :audit/keep again, then sweep.
3. handler-meta {:frame :audit/live :kind :sub :id :audit/value} returns nil, but a fresh subscribe returns the identical cached reaction and derefs to 1.
4. Dispatch :n = 2: that deleted handler still computes 2.

Probe output: :registration-absent true; :cached-reaction-reused true :after 1; :deleted-handler-still-computes 2. This is separate from the documented resource/route cleanup limits: normal SPA subscription views can silently keep behavior the programmer just deleted.

Small fix: invalidate the removed sub's cache and declared dependents in affected live-store frames, reusing the existing invalidation primitive. Preserve unrelated cached subscriptions and the existing explicit-image refresh behavior. No new configuration or lifecycle API.

Acceptance: a reload deleting an already-materialized sub removes its registration and cached entry; a subsequent subscribe or dependent rebuild follows the missing-sub contract, rather than returning the deleted computation. Keep an unrelated subscription as a control.

title: Fresco docs promise caret-and-selection preservation and a mount-local virtual clock; state the end-relative caret rule and the page-wide clock
description:
Two pieces of Fresco documentation promise more than the code does. This is docs and docstrings only, with no code change.

## 1. Caret and selection

`converge-to!` in `implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/controlled.cljs` computes `offset (- (count dom-value) caret-was)` from `selectionStart` alone, then calls `(.setSelectionRange node c c)`. The result is one collapsed caret at the same distance from the end of the committed value; direction is ignored.

These texts claim more:
- `docs/core/fresco/04-controlled-inputs.md:38`: "**Caret and selection are preserved** when the model rejects or rewrites an edit, including edits in the middle of a string". The same claim recurs at ~L117 and ~L310-311.
- `docs/core/fresco/glossary.md` (~L249).
- `docs/core/fresco/10-native-tier.md` (~L139).
- `implementation/fresco/spec/invariants.md` I15, and its owner `docs/design/fresco/product/specification.md` (~L166). I15's row defers to that owner, so the two move together.

State the policy in the present tense: the caret keeps its distance from the end of the committed text, and a selected range comes back collapsed. Keep the `email`/`number` note.

Do NOT add range preservation, a caret-policy option or a formatter hook; no caller needs one.

## 2. The test kit's virtual clock

The namespace docstring of `implementation/fresco/test_kit/src/re_frame/fresco/test/mounted.cljs` says, in "Time is OPT-IN, and it is a mount's own window", that "**It is the mount's window and nothing wider.** … Nothing outside that window is affected, and no mount that did not ask gets one."

In fact `install-clock!` replaces `globalThis` `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout`, `clearInterval` and `Date.now`, holder-counted in one `(defonce ^:private !clock (atom nil))`. So:
- while any clocked mount is open, every timer on the page is virtual;
- `advance-clock!` on one handle fires all due timers.

The file's own comment already says "Page-wide".

Rewrite that section and the `:clock` option text in `mount!` to state the page-wide scope, and add one sentence to "Virtual clock behaviour" in `docs/core/fresco/15-testing.md`.

Also: `mount!` renders through the private `catching-root!` under a frame `mint-frame!` made. It therefore never runs `h/render!` or `h/frame-root`'s ENSURE. Add one sentence calling it a leaf mount, and point at `implementation/fresco/test/re_frame/fresco/public_root_lifecycle_dom_cljs_test.cljs`, which witnesses public boot.

## Files and gates

All the files are `w/crlf`: edit with the Edit/Write tools, not sed. No hot-zone file.

title: Unit-test pruning: epoch
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/epoch/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/epoch/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/epoch/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/epoch/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/epoch/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/epoch/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already

title: Handle whole-vector redaction when rebuilding snapshot trace bundles
description: PR #11362 adds project-trace-bundles-src in tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/epoch_egress.cljs:403-409. It always reduces absorb over pe#, assuming the epoch projector returns a sequence. The actual projection contract also permits a whole-value :rf/redacted sentinel. A focused JVM probe using core/epoch sources archived exactly at merged SHA 5a8e5613719626d88d197f161f8b0c487622bfb3, and the actual source-renderer functions read from that SHA, reproduces this with a live frame classified by apply-classification-effects {:sensitive [[]]}. Ordinary-frame control returns [:login :rf/redacted] with no secret. With root sensitivity, project-egress returns :trace-events :rf/redacted, then the new bundle rebuild throws IllegalArgumentException: Don't know how to create ISeq from: clojure.lang.Keyword. Thus a legitimate privacy classification makes snapshot fail instead of safely returning redacted data. Probe: ai/pr-audit/11362-behavior-probe.clj and its .log in the audit worktree (runner exit 0; the observed exception is caught and printed). Small correction: distinguish sequential projected events from a projected sentinel/marker before folding. Keep the projected slot and safe empty/redacted derived slots for a whole-value result, without reconstructing any slot from original events. Acceptance: a snapshot of a root-sensitive live frame completes with no secret, while ordinary bundle identity and derived-slot consistency remain intact.

== FIX (PR #11373, branch worker/pair-mcp-snapshot-traces, with rf2-ym4z0) ==
project-trace-bundles-src (tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/epoch_egress.cljs) now folds absorb only when the projected :trace-events is sequential?. A whole-slot answer (:rf/redacted from a {:sensitive [[]]} frame, or any other non-sequential marker) ships as the bundle's :trace-events beside empty-event-bundle's empty domino slots. :dispatch-id and :frame come from the bundle. Nothing is rebuilt from the original events.

title: Spec 009: widen the :rf.schema/violation catalogue row to cover a first reg-app-schema registration over a present non-conforming value
description:
## Ruling

A path schema registered with `reg-app-schema` constrains the value at its path only when that path exists; an absent path is not checked, a present value (`nil` included) is, and an enclosing schema (usually the root `[]`) declares whether a key must exist. As part of that ruling, a FIRST registration now checks a live value that is present and emits `:rf.schema/violation`, as a re-registration with a changed schema already does, and every registration skips an absent value. The implementation and the `spec/010-Schemas.md` text land in the schemas bead this one depends on. This bead brings the Spec 009 error-event catalogue into line, and is split out only because `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` is a hot-zone file.

Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned. Mike's instruction, verbatim:

> review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section.  Where the original recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision.  And then remove the file.  Leave behind cases where the two differ materially.

Decisive facts, at trunk 89517e8f54:

1. The `:rf.schema/violation` catalogue row (`spec/009-Instrumentation.md:2002`) describes only the hot-reload edge: "A registered `app-db` path schema changed during hot-reload … and the current `app-db` value at that path no longer validates against the **new** schema". Its tag column defines `:pre-reload-schema` as "the previously-registered schema form", which has no value on a first registration.
2. Today a first registration emits nothing because `maybe-emit-schema-violation!` is gated on `prior-registered?` (`implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/storage.cljc:536-538`). The schemas bead lifts that gate for a present value, so the catalogue must say the category can now fire on a first registration.

Rejected: leaving the row as it is (the catalogue is the authoritative enumeration that `spec/010-Schemas.md:827` points to, so it would understate when the category fires); a new warning category for the first-registration case (the event is the same drift diagnostic with the same recovery, and the ruling adds no warning category).

Supersedes: nothing beyond the schemas bead's own supersession (the first-registration choice recorded on rf2-mn2ht.14).

## Work

- `spec/009-Instrumentation.md:2002`, the `:rf.schema/violation` row: the trigger cell says the category fires when a re-registration changes the schema and the live value fails it, OR when a first registration finds a present live value that fails the schema; an absent value is never checked. The tags cell says what `:pre-reload-schema` carries on a first registration, matching whatever the schemas bead implemented (read `storage.cljc` `maybe-emit-schema-violation!` after it merges).
- `tools/xray/spec/021-Dynamic-Panel-Designs.md:3290-3294` restates the category as "hot-reload drift: a re-registration changed the schema"; widen it to match. Not a hot zone.
- Check `spec/Conventions.md:117`, which names the op "Hot-reload drift (the `:rf.schema/violation` op, which has no owning pipeline step)". Edit it only if it now misleads; `spec/Conventions.md` is a hot zone, so if you touch it, it joins this bead's sequencing.
- Nothing else changes: no code, no tests.

## Sequencing

- Hot zones: `spec/009-Instrumentation.md`; also `spec/Conventions.md` if the `:117` check leads to an edit. Queue behind any open work in those files.
- Bead dependencies: depends on the schemas bead filed alongside it ("Make an absent app-db path unchecked …"), so the catalogue matches merged behaviour and the `:pre-reload-schema` choice is known. Can run in parallel with the docs-and-examples bead.
- Cross-dossier: other dossiers' work that edits `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` must be sequenced against this; the coordinator wires those links.
- Gates: `mkdocs build --strict` and `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` (spec prose). Nothing validates table column counts, so check the row by hand and say so in the PR body.

## Evidence

Read in source at trunk 89517e8f54: `spec/009-Instrumentation.md:2002`; `spec/010-Schemas.md:827-829`; `storage.cljc:513-574`; `tools/xray/spec/021-Dynamic-Panel-Designs.md:3288-3294`; `spec/Conventions.md:117`. Nothing needs a run beyond the doc gates.

2. The row's tag cell states what `:pre-reload-schema` carries on a first registration, and it matches the merged implementation in `storage.cljc`.
3. `tools/xray/spec/021-Dynamic-Panel-Designs.md` describes the category the same way. `spec/Conventions.md:117` was checked, and either left as is or edited consistently.

Spec 005 Drain semantics Level 2 gains "Machine-emitted fx and their order". It is the one ordering rule the four beads in this cluster share; rf2-2kvvj, rf2-9v3kd and rf2-i3id3 point to it.

A transition's :fx is five groups in a fixed order:
1. the action fx (exit deepest-first, then the transition :action, then entry shallowest-first)
2. :rf.machine/after-cancel, one per exited :after state
3. :rf.machine/destroy, one per exited :spawn / :spawn-all state
4. the spawns: :rf.machine/spawn per entered :spawn; for an entered :spawn-all, :rf.machine/spawn-all-init followed by one spawn per child in :children order
5. :rf.machine/after-schedule, one per :after entry of each entered state

Groups 2-5 take their states outermost first, on exit too. The section also covers:
- a macrostep: its transitions' groups, in the order they ran;
- birth: the root :entry fx, then the root :spawn (invoke-id []), then the descent's groups 1, 4 and 5;
- parallel: one block per region in declaration order; the parallel root's own :after schedules last.

Source: apply-transition-once concatenates fx, after-cancel, destroy, spawn, after-schedule and done (machines/transition.cljc:3873-3878). exited-pairs and entered-pairs run root to leaf (nodes-along-path, :712-733). Running machine-transition and apply-initial-entry-cascade over flat, compound, :spawn-all, parallel and birth probe machines gave exactly this order.

Spec fixed to match the code:
- Composition with hierarchical states said exit destroys run innermost first. The code emits them outermost first, and the spec now says so. Making them innermost first would be a runtime change for its own bead.
- The sibling-vocabulary :rf/parent-id is the actor's own address (registration.cljc:438-447), not the parent's.

The probe's answer is confirmed: on entry, :entry fx then spawn then after-schedule; on exit, :exit fx then after-cancel then destroy (machine-timeout-spawn-fire).

description: Spec-Schemas' footer says standard effects ship with a :schema on their registration, but the machines artefact's effect registrations (implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc ~239-257: :rf.machine/spawn, destroy, after-schedule, after-cancel, spawn-all-init) carry only :doc. notes:
